children.title: Input Representation Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Encoding choices that determine the relevant complexity measure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unary, binary, and arithmetic input-size models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-size and operation-count conventions for positive integer input data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t\in\mathbb N\) with \(t\ge 1\), the unary, binary, and arithmetic input-size charges are respectively \(t\), \(1+\lfloor\log_2 t\rfloor\), and \(1\). In the unary and binary models, arithmetic operations are carried out and charged bitwise; in the arithmetic model, each addition, subtraction, multiplication, or comparison is charged one step. These basic arithmetic operations are polynomial-time under the corresponding conventions, whereas exponentiation need not be polynomial-time because its output length need not be polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive integer contributes its value in unary encoding, its number of binary digits in binary encoding, and one unit in arithmetic encoding. Unary and binary models charge bit-level work, while the arithmetic model assigns unit cost to basic arithmetic and comparisons. Basic arithmetic is polynomial-time under these conventions, but exponentiation can fail this bound because its output may be too long.
assumptions_latex: t\in\mathbb N,\quad t\ge 1.
\text{The arithmetic model assigns unit cost to addition, subtraction, multiplication, and comparison.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{\mathrm{unary}}(t)=t,\qquad L_{\mathrm{binary}}(t)=1+\lfloor\log_2 t\rfloor,\qquad L_{\mathrm{arithmetic}}(t)=1.

children.title: Binary Input Encoding
children.top_down_role: Binary representations of coefficients, bounds, objectives, and dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Input Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical signed binary representation for integral and rational optimization data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(z\), define its binary encoding length by \(\ell_2(z)=1\) if \(z=0\), and \(\ell_2(z)=2+\lfloor\log_2|z|\rfloor\) otherwise, where one bit records the sign. A rational number \(r=p/q\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), is encoded by the pair of signed-binary integers \((p,q)\), with length \(\ell_2(r)=\ell_2(p)+\ell_2(q)\). The binary input length of a finite array is the sum of its entry lengths plus the structural encoding needed to identify its dimensions and positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integers use signed base-two digits; reduced rationals encode numerator and positive denominator. An array’s input length sums entry lengths and structural metadata.
assumptions_latex: \(z,p\in\mathbb Z\) and \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
Rational encodings are reduced: \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A magnitude \(M\) contributes \(\Theta(\log(1+M))\) binary digits.

notation.meaning: reduced rational representation with positive denominator

children.title: Bit-Length Complexity
children.top_down_role: Running-time measurement relative to total binary input length.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Length Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity measured against the binary description length of an optimization instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finitely encoded integer or mixed-integer optimization instance, and let \(L(I)\) denote the number of bits in its binary encoding. An algorithm has polynomial bit-length complexity if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every admissible \(I\), it terminates after at most \(p(L(I))\) elementary bit operations and every intermediate number has an encoding of length at most \(p(L(I))\). Under this convention, arithmetic on unbounded integers or rationals is charged according to operand bit length rather than as a unit-cost operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial bit complexity bounds both bit operations and intermediate number sizes by a polynomial in the instance’s binary encoding length.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) has a finite binary encoding.
Arithmetic cost depends on operand bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource bound is polynomial in \(L(I)\), not in the numerical magnitudes represented by \(I\).

children.title: Magnitude Compression Effects
children.top_down_role: Complexity consequences of representing large numeric values compactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude Compression Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential compression of numeric magnitude under binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\), the nonnegative integers \(0,1,\ldots,M\) require at most \(1+\lfloor\log_2 M\rfloor\) magnitude bits each in binary, whereas writing \(M\) unit symbols requires \(M\) symbols. Consequently, a running-time bound polynomial in \(M\) can be exponential in the binary length \(L=\Theta(\log(1+M))\). For example, a bound \(O(M^k)\), with fixed \(k>0\), becomes \(2^{O(L)}\) after expressing magnitude as a function of binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary notation represents magnitude exponentially compactly, so time polynomial in a numeric value may be exponential in that value’s bit length.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\).
\(k>0\) is fixed independently of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial dependence on \(M\) does not generally imply polynomial dependence on \(L=\Theta(\log(1+M))\).

notation.meaning: binary length associated with the magnitude

children.title: Unary Input Encoding
children.top_down_role: Unary representations of numeric coefficients, capacities, and bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Unary Input Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-symbol encoding for nonnegative integral magnitudes, with an explicit sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z\in\mathbb Z\), a unary encoding consists of a sign symbol followed by \(|z|\) copies of a unit symbol; zero is represented by the sign symbol and no unit symbols. Its length is therefore \(\ell_1(z)=1+|z|\). A finite integer array is encoded by concatenating entry encodings with delimiters and dimension metadata. Thus an entry of magnitude \(M\) occupies \(\Theta(M)\) symbols, in contrast to the \(\Theta(\log(1+M))\) digits required by binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary encoding writes an integer’s magnitude using one symbol per unit, so its length grows linearly with magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\mathbb Z\).
Delimiters and dimension metadata use a fixed unambiguous convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unary encoding length satisfies \(\ell_1(z)=\Theta(1+|z|)\).

notation.meaning: unary encoding length of an integer

children.title: Magnitude-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Runtime dependence on represented numeric magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Running-time bounds parameterized by numeric magnitudes as well as combinatorial dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an integer optimization instance, let \(L(I)\) be its binary length, and let \(M(I)\) be the maximum absolute value of its integral numerical data. A magnitude-sensitive running-time bound has the form \(T(I)\le p(L(I),M(I))\) for some polynomial \(p\). Such a bound is polynomial under unary encoding because the unary input length is at least \(M(I)\), but it need not be polynomial under binary encoding, where \(M(I)\) may be exponential in \(L(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A magnitude-sensitive bound is polynomial in dimensions or bit length and also in the largest numeric value; it is generally only pseudo-polynomial for binary input.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) contains finitely many integral numerical entries.
\(M(I)=\max\{|a|:a\text{ is integral data in }I\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial dependence on \(M(I)\) is polynomial for unary input but may be exponential for binary input.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the instance

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Frontier
children.top_down_role: Regimes where numeric magnitude controls the transition to polynomial behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating polynomial bit complexity from polynomial dependence on encoded magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) range over a class of binary-encoded instances, let \(L(I)\) be the binary input length, and let \(M(I)\) be the largest relevant integral magnitude. Suppose an algorithm has running time \(T(I)\le p(L(I),M(I))\), where \(p\) is a fixed polynomial that is nondecreasing on nonnegative arguments. Such a magnitude-dependent guarantee is pseudo-polynomial when it does not yield a polynomial bound solely in \(L(I)\). A sufficient condition for polynomial bit complexity is that \(M(I)\le q(L(I))\) throughout the instance class for some polynomial \(q\). Another sufficient route is an independently established bound polynomial in \(L(I)\) and \(\log(1+M(I))\), because the binary encoding of the datum attaining \(M(I)\) has length \(\Theta(\log(1+M(I)))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A magnitude-dependent polynomial bound is pseudo-polynomial when it does not provide a polynomial bound in binary input length alone. It does provide polynomial bit complexity if the relevant magnitudes are polynomially bounded in input length, or if a separate bound depends only polynomially on their logarithms.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is binary encoded and contains finitely many integral numerical data.
\(p\) is a fixed polynomial nondecreasing on nonnegative arguments.
\(L(I)\) denotes total binary input length and \(M(I)\) the largest relevant integral magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial dependence on \(M(I)\) may be exponential in \(L(I)\); the stated conditions are sufficient, but not asserted to be necessary, for polynomial bit complexity.

children.title: Rational Input Data
children.top_down_role: Representation costs associated with rational coefficients, bounds, and objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Input Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exact rational data for linear integer and mixed-integer optimization instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational-data optimization instance is one whose explicitly supplied objective, constraint, bound, and right-hand-side coefficients belong to \(\mathbb Q\). Each coefficient is represented exactly as \(p/q\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\). Its numerical input size is the sum of the binary lengths of all numerators and denominators; consequently, arithmetic and complexity claims must account for both numerator and denominator growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational input data consist of exact reduced fractions. Their encoding size counts both numerator and denominator bits across all supplied coefficients.
assumptions_latex: The instance has finitely many explicitly supplied numerical coefficients.
Every rational coefficient is stored exactly in reduced form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The numerical encoding length is \(\sum_j\bigl(\ell_2(p_j)+\ell_2(q_j)\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: reduced representation of the j-th rational datum

children.title: Integral Input Data
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes restricted to integer-valued input data.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Input Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization instances whose explicit numerical coefficients are integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integral-data optimization instance is one whose explicitly supplied objective, constraint, bound, and right-hand-side coefficients all belong to \(\mathbb Z\). This classification concerns the numerical data, not the variable domains: an integral-data model may contain continuous, integer, or mixed variable domains. Under binary encoding, its numerical input length is the sum of the signed binary lengths of these integer coefficients, together with the structural description length of the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral input data means every supplied coefficient is an integer; it does not mean every decision variable must be integer-valued.
assumptions_latex: The model contains finitely many explicit coefficients.
All such coefficients belong to \(\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the integral data are \(a_1,\ldots,a_N\), their numerical length is \(\sum_{j=1}^N\ell_2(a_j)\).

children.title: Mixed Numeric Data
children.top_down_role: Instances combining rational and integral components across model elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Numeric Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization data containing both integral and nonintegral rational coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-numeric-data instance is an exactly encoded optimization instance whose supplied coefficient set \(D\) satisfies \(D\subseteq\mathbb Q\), \(D\cap\mathbb Z\ne\varnothing\), and \(D\setminus\mathbb Z\ne\varnothing\). Integral entries are encoded as signed binary integers, while nonintegral entries are encoded as reduced numerator-denominator pairs. This numeric classification is independent of mixed-integer variable domains: “mixed” here describes coefficient types, whereas mixed-integer optimization describes the coexistence of discrete and continuous decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed numeric data contain both integer coefficients and genuinely fractional rational coefficients; this is distinct from having mixed continuous and integer variables.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the finite set of explicitly supplied coefficients.
Every member of \(D\) is represented exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mixed numeric data satisfy \(D\subseteq\mathbb Q\), \(D\cap\mathbb Z\ne\varnothing\), and \(D\setminus\mathbb Z\ne\varnothing\).

children.title: Denominator Clearing Effects
children.top_down_role: Input-size consequences of converting rational data to integral form.

knowledge_statements.title: Denominator Clearing Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence and encoding growth caused by scaling rational linear inequalities to integral form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a rational inequality \(a^\top x\le b\), and write every coefficient of \((a,b)\) in reduced form. Let \(Q\) be any positive common multiple of their denominators. Multiplication by \(Q\) yields the equivalent integral inequality \((Qa)^\top x\le Qb\). If the denominators are \(q_1,\ldots,q_s\), choosing \(Q=\operatorname{lcm}(q_1,\ldots,q_s)\) gives \(\log_2 Q\le\sum_{j=1}^s\log_2 q_j\); hence denominator clearing may greatly increase coefficient magnitudes but increases their binary lengths by at most a polynomial amount in the original rational encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a rational inequality by a positive common denominator preserves its feasible set. Coefficients may become large, but their bit lengths remain polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: The inequality has finitely many rational coefficients.
The scaling factor \(Q\) is a positive common multiple of all coefficient denominators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(a^\top x\le b\) and \((Qa)^\top x\le Qb\) are equivalent, with \(\log_2 Q\le\sum_{j=1}^s\log_2 q_j\) for the least-common-multiple choice.

notation.meaning: positive common denominator used for scaling
reduced denominator of the j-th coefficient

children.title: Explicit Polyhedral Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Polyhedra supplied through finite inequality or equality systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Polyhedral Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inequality-and-equality representation of a rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit rational polyhedral description presents a set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) by finite rational arrays \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), \(C\in\mathbb Q^{r\times n}\), and \(d\in\mathbb Q^r\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}.\] Its encoding length includes \(m,n,r\), the positions and relation types, and the binary lengths of every rational entry. Equalities may equivalently be replaced by paired inequalities, changing description length by only a polynomial factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit polyhedral representation lists finitely many rational linear inequalities and equalities, with complexity measured by dimensions, structure, and coefficient bit lengths.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n,r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
All entries of \(A,b,C,d\) are exactly encoded rationals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The represented set is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\).

children.title: Separation-Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral access through separating-hyperplane queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation oracle for a closed convex set under rational query encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. A strong separation oracle receives a rational query point \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\). It either certifies \(y\in K\), or returns rational \(a\in\mathbb Q^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb Q\) satisfying \(a^\top x\le\beta<a^\top y\) for every \(x\in K\). Polynomial-time separation-oracle access additionally requires the oracle’s running time and the binary lengths of \((a,\beta)\) to be polynomially bounded in the query length and the specified encoding parameters of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle accepts a rational point and either confirms membership or returns a rational hyperplane strictly separating that point from the closed convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The query satisfies \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns membership or \((a,\beta)\) with \(a^\top x\le\beta<a^\top y\) for all \(x\in K\).

notation.meaning: closed convex set accessed through the oracle

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. Moreover, rational separating output and polynomial output-size guarantees require an appropriate rational or well-described-set model; they do not follow from nonempty closed convexity alone.

children.top_down_role: Polyhedral access limited to membership queries.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Q}^n\) is accessed only through oracle queries.
Query points have rational binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_S(y)=1\iff y\in S\).

notation.meaning: membership oracle for the represented set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership access; no separation witness or distance guarantee is implicit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A membership-oracle representation of a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Q}^n\) is a procedure \(M_S\) that, for every rational query point \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), returns \(M_S(y)\in\{0,1\}\) with \(M_S(y)=1\) exactly when \(y\in S\). Its query complexity counts calls to \(M_S\), while bit complexity additionally counts computation on the binary encoding of \(y\). A negative answer certifies only nonmembership; it need not provide a separating inequality, a violated constraint, or a quantitative distance from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A membership oracle answers whether a rational point belongs to the represented set, but a negative answer need not supply a separating inequality or other witness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact membership access to \(K\) does not by itself furnish a polynomial-time exact separation oracle: from the bit \(y\notin K\), no rational separating hyperplane or bound on its encoding length follows. The standard equivalence instead uses weak oracles and quantitative geometry. If rational data certify \(B(a,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(a,R)\), with \(R/r\) polynomially bounded in the encoded parameters, then weak membership, weak separation, and weak linear optimization are polynomial-time interreducible at polynomially related tolerances. Removing well-boundedness, tolerance, or encoding-size promises invalidates that equivalence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact membership is weaker than exact separation without additional promises. Polynomial equivalence applies to weak oracles for quantitatively well-bounded convex bodies.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary belongs in this leaf and failure_boundary is appropriate, but the formal claim that exact membership and exact separation are not polynomially equivalent requires a precisely specified oracle model and direct source support. The stated well-boundedness assumptions also do not define the weak-oracle tolerances or encoding parameters sufficiently to verify the interreducibility claim.

children.title: Computational Task Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Decision, search, optimization, representation, counting, and enumeration tasks whose reductions and output models differ.

children.title: Feasibility Decision
children.top_down_role: Complexity of deciding whether an admissible integer point exists.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\) are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{FEAS}(A,b)=\mathrm{YES}\iff\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-encoded pure integer linear feasibility in variable dimension.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary-encoded \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), integer linear feasibility is the decision problem that returns \(\mathrm{YES}\) precisely when \(F(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty, and returns \(\mathrm{NO}\) otherwise. The output contains no feasible point and no infeasibility certificate unless the task interface explicitly requests one. Input length is the total binary encoding length of \(A\), \(b\), and the dimensions.

children.title: Feasible-Point Search
children.top_down_role: Complexity of producing an admissible integer point.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\) are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(A,b)=\varnothing\Rightarrow\text{output }\mathrm{INFEASIBLE};\quad F(A,b)\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\text{output some }x\in F(A,b).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search interface for binary-encoded integer linear systems.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given binary-encoded \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), feasible-point search is the task defined by \(F(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\). If \(F(A,b)=\varnothing\), its required output is \(\mathrm{INFEASIBLE}\); otherwise its required output is an explicitly encoded vector \(x\in F(A,b)\). Correctness requires every reported vector to satisfy all inequalities and integrality exactly. A polynomial-time solution to the search task must run in time polynomial in the input length, which in particular requires the produced vector to have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible-point search is the task of returning an exactly verifiable integer solution or reporting infeasibility; a polynomial-time solution must also produce a polynomial-size output.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Point Search

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(A,b,c)=\sup\{c^\top x:x\in\mathbb{Z}^n,\ Ax\le b\}\), with explicit infeasible and unbounded outcomes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximization of a linear objective over a pure integer feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given binary-encoded \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), exact objective optimization is the task defined on \(F(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\). Its required output is \(\mathrm{INFEASIBLE}\) when \(F(A,b)=\varnothing\), \(\mathrm{UNBOUNDED}\) when \(\sup\{c^\top x:x\in F(A,b)\}=+\infty\), and otherwise the finite optimum value together with an optimizer \(x^*\in F(A,b)\) satisfying \(c^\top x^*=\max\{c^\top x:x\in F(A,b)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact integer optimization is the task of reporting infeasibility, unboundedness, or a finite optimum together with an integer optimizer attaining it.

children.title: Task-Reduction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation and oracle conditions governing reductions among the three tasks.

assumptions_latex: Instances are rational or integer linear systems with binary encoding.
Whenever a finite optimum exists, relevant solution and objective values have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{search}\le_T^p\mathrm{decision}\) and \(\mathrm{optimization}\le_T^p\mathrm{decision}\) only under polynomial encodability and suitable boundedness promises.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of decision, search, and optimization reductions under binary encoding.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 10. Sizes and the theoretical complexity of linear inequalities and linear programming p. 120
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Optimization yields feasibility by optimizing the zero objective, and a returned optimizer yields a feasible point. Conversely, reductions from feasibility decision to search or optimization require additional structure. Coordinate fixing or binary search can recover a point or optimum using polynomially many decision queries when polynomial bounds on coordinate and objective encodings are available. Without such bounds, the query interval or output itself may have exponential encoding length. These are Turing reductions; they do not imply many-one reductions, parsimonious reductions, or polynomial-delay enumeration, and they must separately handle infeasibility and unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization directly subsumes feasibility and search, but reverse polynomial reductions need bounded, polynomial-size values and generally use adaptive oracle queries.
knowledge_statements.title: Task-Reduction Boundaries

children.top_down_role: Access models returning objective optima over represented regions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a rational polyhedron represented by the oracle.
Objective vectors are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_K(c)\in\{\mathrm{EMPTY},\mathrm{UNBOUNDED}\}\cup K\), and whenever a point is returned it maximizes \(c^\top x\) over \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact linear-optimization oracle for a rational polyhedron \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) accepts any binary-encoded \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). It returns \(\mathrm{EMPTY}\) if \(K=\varnothing\), returns \(\mathrm{UNBOUNDED}\) if \(\sup\{c^\top x:x\in K\}=+\infty\), and otherwise returns a point \(x^*\in K\) satisfying \(c^\top x^*=\max\{c^\top x:x\in K\}\). In a polynomial oracle model, each returned point must have polynomial encoding length; oracle calls and auxiliary bit operations are accounted for according to the stated oracle-cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact optimization oracle maximizes a rational linear objective over a rational polyhedron while explicitly distinguishing empty and unbounded cases.

children.title: Separation-Oracle Interface
children.top_down_role: Access models returning certificates that separate query points from represented regions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a rational polyhedron represented by the oracle.
Queries are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_K(y)=\mathrm{IN}\) if \(y\in K\); otherwise \(S_K(y)=(a,\beta)\) with \(a^\top x\le\beta<a^\top y\) for every \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong rational-separation interface with an explicit violated valid inequality.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strong separation oracle for a rational polyhedron \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) accepts a rational point \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). If \(y\in K\), it returns \(\mathrm{IN}\). Otherwise it returns rational \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\), with \(a\ne0\), such that \(a^\top x\le\beta<a^\top y\) for every \(x\in K\). The returned inequality is a nonmembership certificate relative to the represented set. Polynomial-time strong separation additionally requires polynomial running time and polynomial encoding length of \((a,\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle for a rational polyhedron either confirms membership or returns a rational valid inequality strictly violated by the query point.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Interface

children.top_down_role: Structural settings permitting complexity transfers between optimization and separation.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty rational polytope.
Polynomial encoding bounds for \(P\) and all oracle outputs are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}(P)\equiv_T^p\mathrm{SEP}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational-polytope version of optimization-separation equivalence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty rational polytope equipped with polynomial bounds on the encoding lengths of its defining facial data and oracle outputs. Then exact linear optimization over \(P\) is solvable in oracle-polynomial time given a strong separation oracle for \(P\). Conversely, strong separation for \(P\) is solvable in oracle-polynomial time given an exact linear-optimization oracle for \(P\). The reductions are polynomial-time Turing reductions measured in dimension, rational input length, and the stated representation bounds; they are not representation-free equivalences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a well-encoded rational polytope, exact linear optimization and strong separation simulate each other using polynomially many oracle operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Equivalence Regimes

children.title: Integrality Equivalence Failures
children.top_down_role: Integer-optimization settings where classical polyhedral oracle equivalences break down.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is represented implicitly.
Oracle access is only to points of \(S\), not to its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}(S)=\mathrm{OPT}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) for linear objectives, but separation of arbitrary points from \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is not supplied by membership in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why convex optimization-separation equivalence does not transfer to discrete membership access.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) and any linear objective \(c\), one has \(\sup\{c^\top x:x\in S\}=\sup\{c^\top x:x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\}\). Nevertheless, membership in the discrete set \(S\) is not a separation oracle for \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(S)\): a fractional query \(y\) may lie in \(P_I\) while necessarily satisfying \(y\notin S\), and a negative discrete-membership answer supplies no valid inequality separating \(y\) from \(P_I\). Convex oracle equivalence therefore applies only after access to the integer hull is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear optimization agrees on integer points and their convex hull, but discrete membership cannot separate fractional queries from the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Equivalence Failures

The integer hull is \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I\) may be requested through facets, separation, optimization, or vertices, and these outputs have distinct size-sensitive complexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output interfaces for representing the convex hull of integer-feasible points.

An integer-hull representation task must specify its output interface: an explicit finite inequality description of \(P_I\), a strong separation oracle for \(P_I\), an exact linear-optimization oracle for \(P_I\), or, when bounded, a vertex enumeration. These interfaces encode the same convex set but are not identical output problems; an explicit description or enumeration can require time at least proportional to an exponentially large output.

children.title: Exact Solution Counting
children.top_down_role: Complexity of determining the exact number of feasible integer points.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and finite bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) are binary encoded.
\(\ell\le u\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(A,b,\ell,u)=\left|\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\right|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact counting for a bounded binary-encoded integer linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given binary-encoded \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and finite integer bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) with \(\ell\le u\), exact solution counting outputs the integer \(N(A,b,\ell,u)=|F|\), where \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\). The output is written in binary, and correctness requires equality with the full cardinality rather than an approximation, parity, threshold decision, or enumeration. Explicit finite bounds ensure that \(N(A,b,\ell,u)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact solution counting returns, in binary, the total number of bounded integer solutions rather than approximating, thresholding, or enumerating them.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Solution Counting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded exact-counting definition is mathematically precise and fits the leaf, but the record has no citation. A specific authoritative source locator supporting the exact counting interface and its binary-output convention is required.

children.title: Solution Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Complexity of listing feasible integer points.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines complete, duplicate-free enumeration for a finite integer-program solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an encoded instance \(I\), let \(S(I)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be its finite set of feasible integer solutions. A solution-enumeration algorithm outputs a sequence \(x^1,\ldots,x^N\) and then halts, where \(N=|S(I)|\), such that \(x^i\in S(I)\) for every \(i\), \(x^i\ne x^j\) whenever \(i\ne j\), and \(\{x^1,\ldots,x^N\}=S(I)\). If \(S(I)=\varnothing\), it produces no solution and terminates with an end-of-enumeration signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration outputs every feasible integer solution exactly once and then terminates, including an immediate termination signal when none exist.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) has a finite, explicitly encodable solution set \(S(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x^1,\ldots,x^N\}=S(I)\) and \(x^i\ne x^j\) for \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: finite feasible-solution set of instance I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the Solution Enumeration leaf, but it has no citation with an inspectable locator. Standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for this review.

children.title: Delay-Sensitive Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Enumeration complexity measured through delay between successive outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Sensitive Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard polynomial-delay measure, including preprocessing and termination delay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=|I|\) be the binary input length. An enumerator for \(S(I)\) has polynomial delay if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every instance, the time before the first output, between any two consecutive outputs, and between the last output and termination is at most \(p(L)\). For \(S(I)=\varnothing\), termination occurs within \(p(L)\). The bound depends on input length rather than on the number of solutions already produced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial delay bounds preprocessing, every inter-output interval, and final termination by a polynomial in input length.
assumptions_latex: \(S(I)\) is finite.
Outputs and the end signal are individually recognizable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_N\}\le p(|I|)\) for some polynomial \(p\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial-delay formulation correctly includes preprocessing, inter-output, empty-output, and termination delays and fits the leaf, but no source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Output-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Runtime assessment relative to input size plus generated output.

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures total enumeration time against input plus explicitly encoded output size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) with finite solution set \(S(I)\), define the output length by \(M(I)=\sum_{x\in S(I)}|\operatorname{enc}(x)|\). An enumeration algorithm is output-polynomial if there exists a polynomial \(q\) such that it outputs every member of \(S(I)\) exactly once and terminates within \(q(|I|+M(I))\) computation steps. This total-time requirement does not by itself bound the delay before the first solution or between consecutive solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Output-polynomial enumeration takes polynomial total time in the combined encoded input and complete output length, without necessarily guaranteeing polynomial delay.
assumptions_latex: \(S(I)\) is finite.
\(\operatorname{enc}(x)\) is a fixed binary encoding of solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(I)\le q\bigl(|I|+M(I)\bigr)\) for some polynomial \(q\).

notation.meaning: total encoded length of all outputs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The output-polynomial total-time condition is precise and appropriately distinguished from polynomial delay, but the record lacks a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Hardness Landscape
children.top_down_role: Classical hardness classifications and the boundaries they impose on general algorithms.

children.title: Feasibility Decision Hardness
children.top_down_role: Intractability of deciding integer feasibility in general formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Decision Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical binary-encoded linear integer-feasibility decision problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given rational binary-encoded data \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), deciding whether there exists \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfying \(Ax\le b\) is NP-complete. NP-hardness already holds for the bounded restriction \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Membership in NP uses an integer feasible point of polynomial encoding length whenever the rational system contains an integer point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary-encoded integer linear feasibility is NP-complete, and remains NP-hard when every variable is binary.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are encoded in binary.
The number of variables is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{IPFeas}=\{(A,b):\exists x\in\mathbb Z^n,\ Ax\le b\}\) is NP-complete.

children.title: Feasible-Witness Hardness
children.top_down_role: Intractability associated with producing feasible integer solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Witness Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search hardness for constructing a feasible integer point or correctly reporting infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the total search task that, on input \((A,b)\), returns some \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(Ax\le b\), or returns \(\bot\) exactly when no such point exists. This task is NP-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions, even with \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\): a polynomial-time solver would decide integer feasibility by testing whether its output is \(\bot\). Consequently, such a total witness algorithm cannot run in polynomial time on all instances unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constructing a feasible integer witness while correctly detecting infeasibility is NP-hard, already for binary variables.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are binary encoded.
The algorithm must distinguish infeasibility from feasible instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{IPFeas}\le_T^p\operatorname{IPWitness}\), so polynomial-time total witness construction implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

children.title: Objective Optimization Hardness
children.top_down_role: Intractability of computing optimal values or optimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Optimization Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness of exact linear-objective optimization over binary or general integer feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given binary-encoded \(A,b,c\), the task of returning an optimizer of \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), together with correct infeasibility and unboundedness outcomes, is NP-hard. Hardness persists for bounded binary programs. Indeed, on the restricted instances \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(c=0\), an exact optimization algorithm returns a feasible point precisely when one exists; hence it decides the NP-complete binary integer-feasibility problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact integer linear optimization is NP-hard, even for bounded binary programs; a zero objective already exposes feasibility hardness.
assumptions_latex: \(A,b,c\) are binary encoded.
The optimizer reports infeasibility correctly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{IPFeas}\le_T^p\operatorname{IPOpt}\), and therefore \(\operatorname{IPOpt}\) is NP-hard.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-objective reduction establishes the stated NP-hardness under the given optimizer interface, but the citation does not locate an exact optimization-hardness result. The mathematical role is a theorem rather than a complexity bound.

children.title: Feasibility-to-Optimization Reductions
children.top_down_role: Complexity transfers between feasibility and optimization tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-to-Optimization Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A polynomial reduction using the constant-zero objective and an exact optimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input binary-encoded \((A,b)\). Form the integer program \(\min\{0^Tx:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) and invoke an exact optimization oracle that either returns an optimizer or reports infeasibility. Output feasible if an optimizer \(x^*\) is returned, and output infeasible otherwise. Construction of the zero objective requires polynomial time, every feasible point is optimal, and the oracle is called once; thus integer feasibility reduces to exact integer optimization by a polynomial-time many-one task reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attach a zero objective and call an exact optimizer once; it returns a feasible point exactly when the original system is feasible.
assumptions_latex: The optimization oracle returns a feasible optimizer or a correct infeasibility outcome.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A,b)\mapsto(A,b,0)\) gives \(\operatorname{IPFeas}\le_m^p\operatorname{IPOpt}\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

children.title: Integer-Hull Description Complexity
children.top_down_role: Size and construction complexity of explicit integer-hull descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Description Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total binary size of a rational inequality description of a bounded integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a rational polytope and let \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)\). The inequality-description complexity of \(P_I\) is the minimum total binary encoding length of any rational system \(Dx\le d\) satisfying \(P_I=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Dx\le d\}\). Encoding length includes all numerators, denominators, signs, and dimensions after each inequality is written with relatively prime integer coefficients under a fixed canonical convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer-hull description complexity is the shortest total binary encoding of any rational inequality system defining the hull exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a rational polytope.
\(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dc}(P_I)=\min_{(D,d):\,P_I=\{x:Dx\le d\}}|\operatorname{enc}(D,d)|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Facet Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum per-inequality encoding size in a minimum-threshold description of the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty rational integer hull \(P_I\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its facet complexity \(\varphi(P_I)\) is the least integer \(s\) for which some rational inequality description \(P_I=\{x:Dx\le d\}\) has every row inequality \(D_i x\le d_i\) of binary encoding length at most \(s\). For a full-dimensional polytope one may take an irredundant system of facet-defining inequalities; coefficients are canonically scaled to relatively prime integers before their encoding length is measured.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facet complexity is the smallest uniform bit-length bound permitting every defining inequality of the integer hull to be encoded.
assumptions_latex: \(P_I\) is a nonempty rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi(P_I)=\min_{P_I=\{x:Dx\le d\}}\max_i|\operatorname{enc}(D_i,d_i)|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complexity separation and short validity certificates for integer-hull facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{coNP}\) and the absence of uniformly polynomial certificates establishing the validity of every integer-hull facet inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the set of rational tuples \((A,b,c,\delta)\) for which \(cx\le\delta\) defines a facet of \(P_I\), and let \(V\) be the set for which \(cx\le\delta\) is valid for \(P_I\), where \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\). Then \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{coNP}\) if and only if there is no language \(L\in\mathsf{NP}\) satisfying \(F\subseteq L\subseteq V\); equivalently, the validity of all facet-defining inequalities does not admit uniformly polynomially bounded proofs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NP differs from coNP exactly when there is no NP-verifiable, polynomial-certificate system lying between facet-defining inequalities and all valid integer-hull inequalities.

P=\{x:Ax\le b\}
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)
P_I\ne\varnothing\text{ in the facet-proof formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{coNP}\iff\neg\exists L\in\mathsf{NP}:F\subseteq L\subseteq V

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Vertex Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum encoding length of vertices for a bounded rational integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_I\) be a nonempty rational polytope with vertex set \(V(P_I)\). Its vertex complexity is \(\nu(P_I)=\max\{|\operatorname{enc}(v)|:v\in V(P_I)\}\), where rational coordinates are stored as reduced numerator-denominator pairs under a fixed binary convention. When \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)\) for a rational polytope \(P\), every vertex of \(P_I\) is integral, so this reduces to the maximum binary encoding length of its integer vertex vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex complexity is the largest binary encoding length of any integer-hull vertex under a fixed coordinate encoding.
assumptions_latex: \(P_I\) is a nonempty rational polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(P_I)=\max_{v\in V(P_I)}|\operatorname{enc}(v)|\).

children.title: Vertex Adjacency Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity of recognizing or navigating adjacency in integer-hull graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Adjacency Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial adjacency test when the integer hull is supplied by an explicit inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_I=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Dx\le d\}\) be a full-dimensional rational polytope, and let distinct vertices \(u,v\) be supplied explicitly. Define \(J=\{i:D_i u=d_i\text{ and }D_i v=d_i\}\). Then \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}(D_J)=n-1\). Computing the active rows and their rational rank takes time polynomial in the binary encoding length of \((D,d,u,v)\). This bound assumes that an exact description of the integer hull, rather than merely its original relaxation, is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an explicit full-dimensional integer-hull description, two vertices are adjacent exactly when their common active constraints have rank one below dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(P_I\) is full-dimensional and bounded.
\(D,d,u,v\) are rational and binary encoded.
\(u\) and \(v\) are distinct vertices of \(P_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\sim v\iff\operatorname{rank}(D_J)=n-1\), decidable in polynomial time from \((D,d,u,v)\).

notation.meaning: indices of inequalities active at both vertices
u and v are adjacent vertices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated full-dimensional explicit-description assumptions, the common-active-row rank criterion and polynomial-time rank computation are mathematically sound and fit the leaf. No cited source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Feasibility Hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Feasibility Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical rational linear mixed-integer feasibility with variable dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given binary-encoded rational data \(A,G,b\), deciding whether there exist \(x\in\mathbb Z^p\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^q\) satisfying \(Ax+Gy\le b\) is NP-complete when \(p\) is part of the input. NP-hardness follows already from the restriction \(q=0\), which is integer linear feasibility. Membership in NP follows from the existence, for every feasible rational mixed-integer system, of a feasible pair whose integer and rational coordinates have polynomial binary encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational linear mixed-integer feasibility is NP-complete in variable integer dimension because it contains integer feasibility and admits polynomial-size witnesses.
assumptions_latex: \(A,G,b\) are rational and binary encoded.
The integer-variable dimension \(p\) is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MIPFeas}=\{(A,G,b):\exists(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q,\ Ax+Gy\le b\}\) is NP-complete.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Optimization Hardness
children.top_down_role: Optimization hardness specific to mixed-integrality formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Optimization Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness inherited from binary linear optimization, a subclass of mixed-integer optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and \(K\in\mathbb{Q}\), with all data encoded in binary and \(m,n\) included in the input. Deciding whether there exists \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) such that \(Ax\le b\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le K\) is NP-complete. Consequently, computing \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\) is NP-hard, as is optimization over any mixed-integer problem class containing these binary linear instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary linear objective-threshold problem is NP-complete, and binary linear optimization—and therefore any mixed-integer optimization class containing it—is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and \(K\in\mathbb{Q}\) are encoded in binary.
\(m\) and \(n\) are part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary linear threshold problem is NP-complete, and the corresponding optimization problem is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: Rational constraint matrix and right-hand-side vector.

children.title: Restricted-Constraint Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness persisting under limited constraint structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Constraint Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak NP-completeness with one equality constraint and binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and \(B\), all encoded in binary, deciding whether
\[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i=B,\qquad x_i\in\{0,1\}\]
has a solution is NP-complete. Thus binary integer feasibility is NP-hard even with exactly one linear equality constraint. This restricted problem is weakly NP-complete: the standard dynamic program indexed by partial sums runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(B\), but not necessarily in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One binary linear equality suffices for NP-completeness; the resulting subset-sum formulation nevertheless has a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(B\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Single-equality binary integer feasibility is weakly NP-complete.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset-sum hardness statement is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied. The eventual sourced version should also remove the membership and dynamic-program justification from the statement.

children.title: Restricted-Coefficient Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness persisting under limited coefficient alphabets or magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Coefficient Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness with binary variables and uniformly bounded constraint coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a 3-CNF formula, associate \(x_j\in\{0,1\}\) with each Boolean variable. For every clause \(C\), impose
\[\sum_{j\in P_C}x_j+\sum_{j\in N_C}(1-x_j)\ge 1.\]
The resulting system is feasible exactly when the formula is satisfiable. After expansion, every variable coefficient belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\), and every right-hand side belongs to \(\{-2,-1,0,1\}\). The construction is polynomial and feasibility is in NP; therefore binary integer feasibility remains NP-complete under these coefficient restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary integer feasibility stays NP-complete when all variable coefficients and right-hand sides are bounded by small constants.
assumptions_latex: Each input clause has at most three literals.
All decision variables are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is NP-complete even with coefficients in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and right-hand sides in \(\{-2,-1,0,1\}\).

notation.meaning: Variables appearing positively in clause C.
Variables appearing negated in clause C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-coefficient 3-CNF encoding is plausible and locally appropriate, but the NP-completeness claim lacks cited evidence. The construction and correctness explanation are proof text and should be removed after sourcing.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak NP-Hardness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numeric-complexity definition using binary versus unary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numeric decision problem \(\Pi\) is weakly NP-hard when \(\Pi\) is NP-hard under binary encoding of its integer data, but its unary-encoded restriction is solvable in polynomial time. Equivalently for the usual NP-complete numeric problems, the hardness can depend on exponentially large numerical magnitudes rather than solely on combinatorial dimension. This definition does not assert that every weakly NP-hard problem has a pseudo-polynomial algorithm, although such an algorithm establishes polynomial solvability of the corresponding unary instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak NP-hardness means hardness under compact binary encoding disappears when numerical data are written in unary.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) has explicitly identified nonnegative integer parameters whose encoding may be changed from binary to unary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi\) is weakly NP-hard precisely in the stated binary-hard, unary-polynomial regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the proposed binary-hard/unary-polynomial criterion is narrower than some standard definitions of weak NP-hardness. An authoritative numeric-complexity definition is required to settle the exact formulation and equivalence conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong NP-Hardness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong hardness defined by persistence under polynomially bounded numerical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numeric decision problem \(\Pi\) is strongly NP-hard if some polynomial \(p\) exists such that \(\Pi\) remains NP-hard on instances whose numerical values are bounded by \(p(L)\), where \(L\) denotes the remaining combinatorial input length. Equivalently, under the standard numeric encoding model, the restriction obtained by writing numerical data in unary remains NP-hard. If this restricted problem also belongs to NP, it is strongly NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong NP-hardness persists even when all numerical magnitudes are polynomially bounded, equivalently when numbers are unary encoded.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a numeric decision problem with distinguished integer-valued data.
Reductions and encoding lengths use the standard deterministic polynomial-time model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomially bounded numerical magnitudes do not remove NP-hardness from a strongly NP-hard problem.

notation.meaning: Length of the nonnumeric combinatorial input.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended strong-hardness regime is appropriate, but no citation supports the stated polynomial-bound and unary-encoding equivalence. A source must specify the numeric encoding model and the length relative to which magnitudes are bounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between pseudo-polynomial solvability and strong NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a numeric problem has input length \(L\), maximum numerical magnitude \(M\), and an exact algorithm running in time polynomial in \(L\) and \(M\). On unary-encoded instances, \(M\) is at most polynomial in the encoded input length, so this algorithm is polynomial-time. Therefore a strongly NP-hard problem cannot admit such a pseudo-polynomial algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Weak NP-hardness is compatible with pseudo-polynomial solvability but, by itself, does not imply it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial exact algorithm is compatible with weak hardness but, unless P equals NP, incompatible with strong NP-hardness.
assumptions_latex: The running-time polynomial treats the numerical magnitude \(M\), rather than \(\log M\), as a parameter.
The problem is strongly NP-hard under unary encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pseudo-polynomial exact algorithm would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Binary input length apart from numerical magnitude.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudo-polynomial boundary is standard and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the claim has no source and includes an argument rather than only the boundary statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Dimension Exact Counting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact counting becomes number-of-solutions complete when dimension is input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an integer system \(Ax\ge b\) with \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), computing
\[N(A,b)=\bigl|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\ge b\}\bigr|\]
is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete when \(n\) is part of the input. Membership follows because feasible binary vectors are polynomially verifiable witnesses. Hardness follows parsimoniously from \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\): each clause is represented by the inequality requiring at least one of its positive literals \(x_j\) or negative literals \(1-x_j\) to equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting feasible binary integer points is number-of-solutions complete when the number of variables is not fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are integer and binary encoded.
The dimension \(n\) varies with the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Computing \(N(A,b)\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete under parsimonious polynomial-time reductions.

notation.meaning: Class of functions counting accepting polynomial-time witnesses.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-dimension exact-counting claim is plausible and fits the leaf, but #P-completeness under the stated reduction type requires a specific source. The membership and reduction discussion is proof text.

children.title: Projected Lattice-Point Counting
children.top_down_role: Counting distinct images of integer points under coordinate or linear projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Lattice-Point Counting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct projected points are counted without witness multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+k}\) be a bounded rational polytope and let \(\pi(x,y)=x\) be projection onto the first \(d\) coordinates. The projected lattice-point count is
\[N_{\pi}(P)=\bigl|\pi(P\cap\mathbb Z^{d+k})\bigr|=\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb Z^d:\exists y\in\mathbb Z^k,\ (x,y)\in P\}\bigr|.\]
Each projected vector \(x\) contributes exactly once, regardless of how many integer witnesses \(y\) lie above it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected counting counts each integer first-coordinate vector having at least one integer witness exactly once.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a bounded rational polytope.
\(d,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\pi}(P)\) equals the number of distinct integer vectors admitting an integer lift into \(P\).

notation.meaning: Projection onto the first coordinate block.
Number of distinct projected lattice points.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly distinguishes projected points from witness multiplicity and fits the terminal container, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Existentially Quantified Counting
children.top_down_role: Counting assignments admitted by existentially quantified integer variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Existentially Quantified Counting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting free assignments satisfying an existential integer predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^k\) be finite, and let \(\varphi(x,y)\) be a polynomial-time decidable integer predicate. The existential counting function is
\[N_{\exists}(\varphi;X,Y)=\bigl|\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ \varphi(x,y)\}\bigr|.\]
If \(S=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:\varphi(x,y)\}\), then \(N_{\exists}(\varphi;X,Y)=|\pi_X(S)|\). Thus existential counting is projected counting, not counting all witness pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existential counting counts free assignments with at least one witness, rather than counting all assignment-witness pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite integer sets.
\(\varphi\) is decidable in time polynomial in its encoded arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\exists}(\varphi;X,Y)=|\pi_X(S)|\).

notation.meaning: Number of free assignments satisfying the existential predicate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-set representation of existential counting is coherent and locally appropriate, but it lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Alternating-Quantifier Counting
children.top_down_role: Counting regimes involving multiple quantifier blocks or alternation.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Quantifier Counting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting free assignments after a fixed or input-dependent quantifier prefix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_t\) be finite integer sets, let \(\varphi(x,y_1,\ldots,y_t)\) be a decidable predicate, and let \(Q_i\in\{\exists,\forall\}\) alternate. Define
\[N_Q(\varphi)=\bigl|\{x\in X:Q_1y_1\in Y_1\;Q_2y_2\in Y_2\cdots Q_ty_t\in Y_t,\ \varphi(x,y_1,ldots,y_t)\}\bigr|.\]
The quantified formula is evaluated as a Boolean condition for each \(x\); consequently each satisfying \(x\) is counted once, independently of the number of existential witnesses or universal branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating-quantifier counting counts free assignments for which the entire quantified predicate is true.
assumptions_latex: All quantified domains are finite.
Adjacent quantifiers in the prefix alternate.
\(\varphi\) is decidable on encoded assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_Q(\varphi)\) is the cardinality of the free-assignment set satisfying the quantified formula.

notation.meaning: The i-th existential or universal quantifier.
Count induced by the quantifier prefix.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantified-counting definition lacks a source, and its displayed predicate contains the malformed sequence `y_1,ldots,y_t` instead of a properly delimited LaTeX ellipsis. Both issues must be corrected before acceptance.

children.title: Projection Multiplicity Barriers
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects caused by multiple witnesses mapping to the same projected point.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Multiplicity Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why counting witnesses does not generally recover projection cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite relation \(S\subseteq X\times Y\), define each fiber by \(S_x=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in S\}\). Then
\[|S|=\sum_{x\in\pi_X(S)}|S_x|,\qquad |\pi_X(S)|=\sum_{x\in X}\mathbf 1[|S_x|>0].\]
Hence counting feasible pairs equals counting projected points only when every nonempty fiber is a singleton. More generally, dividing \(|S|\) by a constant is valid only when all nonempty fibers have that known constant cardinality; variable multiplicities obstruct recovery of the projection count from the pair count alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Witness-pair counts weight projected points by fiber size, so varying witness multiplicities prevent recovery of the distinct projection count.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq X\times Y\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Variable nonzero fiber sizes make \(|S|\) insufficient to determine \(|\pi_X(S)|\).

notation.meaning: Set of first coordinates having nonempty fibers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fiber-multiplicity boundary is mathematically coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no source with an inspectable locator supports the record.

children.title: Counting-Value Bit-Length
children.top_down_role: Output-size effects caused by large exact counting values.

knowledge_statements.title: Counting-Value Bit-Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary output length of an exact finite lattice-point count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^d([\ell_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z)\) and let \(N=|S|\). Then
\[0\le N\le M:=\prod_{i=1}^d(u_i-\ell_i+1),\qquad \operatorname{bits}(N)\le\left\lceil\log_2(M+1)\right\rceil,\]
where \(\operatorname{bits}(N)=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\) is the information length of the nonnegative count. Thus an exponentially large collection may have a polynomial-length binary count when the logarithms of the coordinate ranges have polynomial total length; enumeration volume and count-value bit-length are distinct resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary length of a count is logarithmic in the number of possible objects, even when explicit enumeration is exponentially large.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_i,u_i\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\ell_i\le u_i\) for every coordinate.
\(S\) is contained in the displayed finite integer box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bits}(|S|)\le\left\lceil\log_2\left(1+\prod_i(u_i-\ell_i+1)\right)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Number of integer vectors in the enclosing box.
Information-theoretic binary length of nonnegative integer N.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic bound is coherent under the explicitly chosen information-length convention, but no source is supplied. A citation should also confirm or clearly distinguish this convention from encodings in which zero occupies one output bit.

children.title: Enumeration Output Volume
children.top_down_role: Runtime lower bounds arising from the number of listed solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration Output Volume
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound for algorithms explicitly listing every feasible integer solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance of binary length \(L\) have distinct solutions \(S=\{x^{1},\ldots,x^{N}\}\), and require an algorithm to write every solution explicitly. In any sequential bit-cost model, its running time is at least \(\Omega\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}|\operatorname{enc}(x^{j})|\right)\), hence at least \(\Omega(N)\). Consequently, polynomial total time in \(L\) is impossible whenever the explicit output length is superpolynomial in \(L\), irrespective of the complexity of finding an individual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit enumeration requires time at least proportional to the total encoded output, so exponentially many solutions preclude input-polynomial total time.
assumptions_latex: Solutions are distinct and written explicitly.
Running time charges at least one step per emitted bit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T(L)\geq \Omega\!\left(\sum_{x\in S}|\operatorname{enc}(x)|\right)\geq\Omega(N).\]

notation.meaning: explicit binary encoding of a solution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The output-length lower bound is mathematically appropriate for this complexity-bound leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable citation. A source on output-sensitive enumeration complexity or computational bit-cost models is required.

children.title: Polynomial-Delay Barriers
children.top_down_role: Obstacles to bounded delay between successive enumerated solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Delay Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier obtained from the delay before the first enumerated witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(I,y)\) be a polynomially balanced, polynomial-time decidable witness relation. Suppose an enumeration algorithm outputs every \(y\) satisfying \(R(I,y)\), without repetition, and has delay polynomial in \(|I|\) before its first output, between consecutive outputs, and between its last output and termination. Then existence of a witness can be decided in polynomial time by waiting for either the first output or termination. Thus, if deciding \(\exists y\,R(I,y)\) is NP-complete, such an enumerator implies \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial delay would decide witness existence in polynomial time; therefore NP-complete existence problems admit no polynomial-delay enumeration unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is polynomially balanced and polynomial-time decidable.
The delay guarantee includes preprocessing and termination delay.
Witness existence for \(R\) is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R\text{ has a polynomial-delay enumerator}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The barrier is correctly stated under a polynomial-delay definition that includes preprocessing and termination delay, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No citation is supplied for the enumeration-complexity implication.

children.title: Compact Output Representations
children.top_down_role: Compressed representations intended to avoid explicit listing of large solution sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Output Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit representation of a finite solution set by a membership circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set \(S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{d}\), a Boolean circuit \(C\) represents \(S\) when \(S=\{x\in\{0,1\}^{d}:C(x)=1\}\). Its representation length is the encoded circuit size \(|C|\), rather than the explicit-list length \(\sum_{x\in S}d=d|S|\). Hence \(|C|\) may be polynomial in the instance length even when \(|S|\) is exponential. Such compactness alone guarantees neither polynomial-delay enumeration nor polynomial-time counting of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit can encode an exponentially large solution set compactly, although compact membership representation alone does not make counting or enumeration efficient.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a finite subset of \(\{0,1\}^{d}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S=C^{-1}(1),\qquad \text{explicit length}=d|S|,\qquad \text{implicit length}=|C|.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The membership-circuit representation and its limitations match the compact-representation leaf, but the nontrivial claims about counting and polynomial-delay enumeration have no cited source.

children.title: Classical Tractability Islands
children.top_down_role: Tractable regimes that precede the more detailed fixed-dimension and structured-algorithm branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Variable Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lenstra-type tractability for rational linear integer programs in fixed total dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\in\mathbb N\). Given rational binary-encoded data \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^{m}\), and \(c\in\mathbb Q^{d}\), linear integer optimization over \(P\cap\mathbb Z^{d}\), where \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^{d}:Ax\leq b\}\), is solvable in time polynomial in the total input length. The algorithm may return an optimal integer point, infeasibility, or unboundedness. The polynomial degree can be chosen independently of the input, while its constant may depend on the fixed dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear integer programming is polynomial-time solvable when the total number of variables is fixed, with dimension-dependent constants.
assumptions_latex: The dimension \(d\) is fixed.
All input coefficients are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{time}(A,b,c)\leq f(d)\,L^{O(1)},\] where \(L\) is the binary input length.

notation.meaning: rational polyhedron defined by the inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-dimension integer-programming tractability statement and complexity_bound role fit the node, but an authoritative theorem-level locator for the Lenstra-type result is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Integer Linear Optimization in Fixed Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure integer linear optimization with a fixed total number of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed integer n\ge 1, the integer linear programming problem \max\{c^Tx\mid Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\} can be solved in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer linear optimization is polynomial-time solvable when the total number of variables is fixed.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb{Z},\ n\ge 1
n\text{ is fixed}
x\in\mathbb{Z}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{c^Tx\mid Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}\text{ can be solved in polynomial time.}
