children.title: Fixed Integer Dimension with Continuous Variables

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Integer Dimension with Continuous Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial solvability of rational MILP with a fixed number of integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\in\mathbb N\), while allowing \(q\) to vary. Given rational binary-encoded \(A,b,c,d\), the mixed-integer linear program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}y:A(x,y)\leq b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^{p},\ y\in\mathbb R^{q}\}\) is solvable in time \(f(p)L^{O(1)}\), where \(L\) is the total input length. A correct algorithm returns an optimum when finite and attained, and otherwise reports infeasibility or unboundedness. Dependence on \(q\) is polynomial because only the integer dimension is fixed parametrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational mixed-integer linear program is polynomial-time solvable when only the number of integer variables is fixed; continuous dimension may vary.
assumptions_latex: The integer dimension \(p\) is fixed.
The continuous dimension \(q\) may be part of the input.
All data are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{time}(A,b,c,d)\leq f(p)L^{O(1)}.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly distinguishes fixed integer dimension from varying continuous dimension and fits a complexity-bound container. It requires an authoritative theorem locator supporting polynomial-time rational MILP solvability in this regime.

children.title: Bounded-Coefficient Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects of limiting coefficient magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Coefficient Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded matrix coefficients alone do not yield general integer-programming tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Feasibility remains NP-complete for systems \(Ax\leq b\) with \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) even when every entry of \(A\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and every entry of \(b\) has constant absolute value. Therefore, bounding coefficient magnitudes does not by itself provide a polynomial-time regime when the number of variables and constraints, the matrix structure, and binary domains remain unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-sized constraint coefficients do not make general binary integer-program feasibility easy; the problem remains NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: The numbers of variables and constraints are unrestricted.
Variables are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\},\quad \|b\|_{\infty}=O(1)\quad\not\Longrightarrow\quad \text{polynomial-time feasibility}.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated hardness boundary is consistent with bounded-coefficient encodings such as clause inequalities, and failure_boundary is the correct role. No inspectable reduction or theorem citation is supplied.

children.title: Bounded-Right-Hand-Side Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects of limiting right-hand-side magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Right-Hand-Side Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed right-hand side does not control complexity when coefficients remain binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasibility problem \(a^{\mathsf T}x=0\), \(x\in\{-1,1\}^{n}\), with positive binary-encoded integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), is NP-complete by its equivalence to PARTITION. Its sole right-hand side is the fixed constant \(0\). Thus, bounded right-hand sides alone do not imply polynomial-time integer-programming feasibility when coefficient magnitudes and dimension are unrestricted; they do not remove weak NP-hardness caused by binary-encoded coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a zero right-hand side permits NP-complete feasibility through PARTITION when coefficients are unrestricted binary integers.
assumptions_latex: Coefficients \(a_i\) are positive integers encoded in binary.
The dimension \(n\) is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists x\in\{-1,1\}^{n}:a^{\mathsf T}x=0\] is NP-complete despite its fixed right-hand side.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign-vector formulation is equivalent to PARTITION and correctly demonstrates weak NP-completeness with a zero right-hand side. The record nevertheless lacks a citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Bounded Variable Domains
children.top_down_role: Tractability associated with finite or narrowly bounded variable ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Variable Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary domains are bounded but retain general integer-programming hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given rational binary-encoded \(A\) and \(b\), deciding whether \(Ax\leq b\) has a solution \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) is NP-complete. Hence a uniform constant bound on every variable domain does not by itself yield polynomial-time solvability. Tractability requires an additional restriction, such as fixed dimension or special constraint-matrix structure, because the number of binary assignments remains \(2^{n}\) when \(n\) is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting every variable to zero or one still leaves integer-program feasibility NP-complete when dimension and matrix structure are unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: The dimension \(n\) is part of the input.
The constraint system is otherwise unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_i\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for all }i\quad\not\Longrightarrow\quad \text{polynomial-time feasibility}.\]

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

children.title: Combined Numeric Bounds
children.top_down_role: Regimes parameterized by several simultaneous numeric limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Numeric Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous constant numeric bounds remain insufficient without structural restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Binary integer feasibility remains NP-complete for families satisfying \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}\), and \(\|b\|_{\infty}\leq 2\). Such families arise from clause inequalities for 3-SAT. Therefore, simultaneously bounding variable domains, constraint coefficients, and right-hand sides by universal constants does not ensure tractability when dimension, constraint count, and incidence structure are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even simultaneous constant bounds on domains, coefficients, and right-hand sides leave general feasibility NP-complete without structural restrictions.
assumptions_latex: The numbers of variables and constraints are unrestricted.
No structural restriction is imposed on the constraint-variable incidence pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\{0,1\}^{n},\quad \|A\|_{\infty}\leq1,\quad \|b\|_{\infty}\leq2\] still permits NP-complete feasibility.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Clause inequalities for 3-SAT can satisfy the stated constant bounds, so the mathematical boundary and content kind are appropriate. An inspectable source for the bounded 3-SAT-to-binary-IP encoding is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Dynamic-Programming Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-indexed dynamic programming for zero-one knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For item weights \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), values \(v_i\in\mathbb Z\), and capacity \(B\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\), initialize \(D_0(t)=0\) for \(0\leq t\leq B\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), set \(D_i(t)=D_{i-1}(t)\) when \(t<w_i\), and otherwise set \(D_i(t)=\max\{D_{i-1}(t),D_{i-1}(t-w_i)+v_i\}\). Output \(D_n(B)\), optionally recovering selected items by backtracking. The running time is \(O(nB)\) and memory can be \(O(B)\); this is pseudo-polynomial because \(B\) is numeric rather than bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-indexed knapsack dynamic programming runs in O(nB), polynomial in the numeric capacity but potentially exponential in its binary length.
assumptions_latex: Weights are positive integers.
Capacity \(B\) is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_n(B)=\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_ix_i:\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_ix_i\leq B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\right\},\quad T=O(nB).\]

notation.meaning: best value using the first i items at capacity t
weight and value of item i

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Relaxation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness of linear relaxation over an integral rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}\) be a rational integral polyhedron, meaning \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^{n})\). For every rational objective \(c\) whose minimum over \(P\) is finite and attained, the linear relaxation and integer program have equal optimal values, and an integer optimum exists. Consequently, optimizing over \(P\cap\mathbb Z^{n}\) reduces to linear programming whenever an integral description of \(P\) is available with polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the relaxation polyhedron equals the convex hull of its integer points, linear programming returns the integer-program optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is rational and integral.
The objective minimum over \(P\) is finite and attained.
The description of \(P\) has polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=\min_{x\in P\cap\mathbb Z^{n}}c^{\mathsf T}x,\] and the right-hand minimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Variable Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension parameter counting both integer and continuous coordinates in a MILP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mixed-integer linear program with decision vector \((x,y)\in\mathbb Z^{p}\times\mathbb R^{q}\), its total variable dimension is \(d=p+q\). This parameter counts all scalar decision coordinates, independently of the number of constraints, coefficient magnitudes, or encoding length. Fixing \(d\) therefore fixes both the integer-variable dimension \(p\) and the continuous-variable dimension \(q\), whereas fixing \(p\) alone permits \(q\) to grow with the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total variable dimension is the sum of integer and continuous variable counts; fixing it bounds both types simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: The decision space is partitioned as \(\mathbb Z^{p}\times\mathbb R^{q}\).

Its integer-variable dimension is the parameter \(p:=\dim(z)\), equivalently the cardinality of the designated index set \(I:=\{j:x_j\text{ is required to be integral}\}\). Thus \(p=|I|\); fixed-parameter statements in this dimension hold \(p\) fixed while allowing the continuous dimension and encoded input length to vary.

The count concerns variable type, independently of bounds, eliminability, or the rank of the constraint matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a mixed-integer formulation have \(p\) integer variables and \(q\) continuous variables. Its total dimension is \(n=p+q\). Consequently, bounding \(n\) bounds both type-specific dimensions, whereas bounding only \(p\) permits unbounded \(q\), and bounding only \(q\) permits unbounded \(p\). Thus the regimes ``fixed total dimension,'' ``fixed integer dimension,'' and ``fixed continuous dimension'' are distinct parameter restrictions; neither type-specific bound implies a total-dimension bound without a bound on the other block.

notation.meaning: Codimension of the affine solution set in the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine codimension induced by a consistent system of linear equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) and suppose \(F:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}\) is nonempty. The codimension parameter of this equality-defined affine space is \(\operatorname{codim}(F):=n-\dim(F)\). Since every solution set is a translate of \(\ker(A)\), rank-nullity gives \(\operatorname{codim}(F)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\). For inequality systems this identity applies to the affine hull of the feasible set only after its defining equalities are identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consistent equality system, feasible affine codimension equals the rank of its coefficient matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) of rank \(r\), define the row deficiency \(\delta_{\mathrm{row}}:=m-r\) and column deficiency \(\delta_{\mathrm{col}}:=n-r\). The matrix has full row rank exactly when \(\delta_{\mathrm{row}}=0\) and full column rank exactly when \(\delta_{\mathrm{col}}=0\). A bounded-rank-deficiency regime fixes or bounds either deficit while allowing \(m\) or \(n\) to grow; the two regimes are not interchangeable unless the matrix shape is controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row and column rank deficiencies are row count minus rank and column count minus rank; boundedness of one need not bound the other.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Block Dimensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensions induced by a fixed row-and-column block partition of an integer-programming matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) have row partition \((R_i)_{i=1}^{p}\) and column partition \((C_j)_{j=1}^{q}\). children.title: Block-Type Count

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Type Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of distinct block signatures in a specified block-structured integer-programming formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider blocks indexed by \(k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\). Assign each block a signature \(\sigma_k\) containing precisely the local data declared type-relevant, such as its local constraint matrix, variable bounds, right-hand side, and objective coefficients. Define \(k\sim \ell\) if and only if \(\sigma_k=\sigma_\ell\). The block-type count is the number \(\tau=|\{\sigma_k:1\le k\le N\}|\) of equivalence classes. Consequently, \(1\le\tau\le N\); the value of \(\tau\) depends on which local data the formulation declares part of a type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The block-type count is the number of distinct prescribed local-data signatures among all blocks.
assumptions_latex: Each block \(k\) has a well-defined type signature \(\sigma_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau=|\{\sigma_k:1\le k\le N\}|\) and \(1\le\tau\le N\).

children.title: Repetition Count
children.top_down_role: Complexity dependence on the number of repeated blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Repetition Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity data for block types under a fixed block-signature convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) blocks have signatures \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_N\), and let \(T=\{\sigma_k:1\le k\le N\}\). For each type \(t\in T\), its repetition count is \(r_t=|\{k:\sigma_k=t\}|\). The repetition vector is \((r_t)_{t\in T}\), the maximum repetition is \(r_{\max}=\max_{t\in T}r_t\), and \(\sum_{t\in T}r_t=N\). Thus repetition counts measure multiplicity separately from the number and dimensions of distinct block types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A type’s repetition count is its multiplicity among the blocks; all type multiplicities sum to the total block count.
assumptions_latex: Each block \(k\) has a fixed signature \(\sigma_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_t=|\{k:\sigma_k=t\}|\) and \(\sum_{t\in T}r_t=N\).

children.title: Uniformity Across Blocks
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes determined by exact or bounded variation among repeated blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Across Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniformity under a declared block-signature convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For blocks \(k=1,\ldots,N\) with type signatures \(\sigma_k\), exact uniformity across blocks holds if and only if \(\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\cdots=\sigma_N\). Equivalently, the block-type count is \(\tau=1\), or the unique type has repetition count \(N\). Uniform dimensions alone do not imply this condition unless dimensions constitute the entire declared signature; coefficients, bounds, right-hand sides, and objectives must also agree whenever they are included in \(\sigma_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Blocks are exactly uniform when all declared local-data signatures coincide, equivalently when one type occurs N times.
assumptions_latex: The same signature convention is applied to every block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_N\iff\tau=1\iff r_{\mathrm{unique}}=N\).

children.title: Primal Interaction Graph
children.top_down_role: Variable-side graph structure induced by shared constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Interaction Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-intersection graph of an integer-programming constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), the primal interaction graph \(G_P(A)\) is the simple graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), one vertex per variable. Distinct vertices \(j\) and \(k\) are adjacent exactly when some constraint contains both variables with nonzero coefficients: \(\{j,k\}\in E(G_P(A))\) if and only if there exists \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that \(A_{ij}\ne0\) and \(A_{ik}\ne0\). Thus every row support induces a clique in \(G_P(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables are adjacent in the primal graph precisely when they occur together with nonzero coefficients in some constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Incidence Graph Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite support graph whose one-mode projections recover primal and dual interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), define the incidence graph \(G_I(A)\) as the bipartite graph with constraint vertices \(R=\{r_1,\ldots,r_m\}\), variable vertices \(C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}\), and edge \(\{r_i,c_j\}\) exactly when \(A_{ij}\ne0\). Two variable vertices have a common neighbor in \(G_I(A)\) exactly when they are adjacent in \(G_P(A)\); two constraint vertices have a common neighbor exactly when they are adjacent in \(G_D(A)\). Hence the primal and dual graphs are the respective simple two-section projections of \(G_I(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence graph records nonzeros bipartitely; projecting common-neighbor relations onto variables or constraints yields the primal or dual graph.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_P(A)=\operatorname{2sec}_{C}(G_I(A))\) and \(G_D(A)=\operatorname{2sec}_{R}(G_I(A))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Parameter Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded separation between corresponding primal and dual width parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n\) be the \(1\times n\) all-ones matrix. Then \(G_P(A_n)=K_n\), while \(G_D(A_n)=K_1\); hence their treewidths are \(n-1\) and \(0\), and their treedepths are \(n\) and \(1\). For the transpose \(A_n^{\mathsf T}\), these roles reverse. Therefore neither primal treewidth nor primal treedepth is bounded by any function of the corresponding dual parameter alone, and neither dual parameter is bounded by any function of its primal counterpart alone.

children.title: Primal Graph Treewidth

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Graph Treewidth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treewidth parameter applied to the primal interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_P(A)=(V,E)\). A tree decomposition is a tree \(T\) with bags \((B_t)_{t\in V(T)}\), where \(B_t\subseteq V\), such that every vertex lies in a bag, each edge has both endpoints in some bag, and \(\{t:v\in B_t\}\) is connected in \(T\) for every \(v\in V\). The primal graph treewidth is \(\operatorname{tw}_P(A)=\min_{(T,B)}(\max_t|B_t|-1)\), with the minimum over all tree decompositions of \(G_P(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal graph treewidth is the minimum tree-decomposition bag size minus one for the variable interaction graph.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
\(G_P(A)\) is the primal interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tw}_P(A)=\operatorname{tw}(G_P(A))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Graph Treedepth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treedepth parameter applied to the primal interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted forest \(F\), its closure \(\operatorname{cl}(F)\) joins each vertex to every proper ancestor. Equivalently, every primal edge must connect an ancestor-descendant pair in \(F\).

\(G_P(A)\) is the primal interaction graph.

children.title: Treewidth–Treedepth Separation
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions between bounded-treewidth and bounded-treedepth regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Treewidth–Treedepth Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation for finite undirected graphs under the convention that a single vertex has treedepth one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty finite undirected graph \(G\), treewidth and treedepth satisfy \(\operatorname{tw}(G)+1\leq \operatorname{td}(G)\). The converse admits no constant bound: for the path \(P_n\) on \(n\geq 2\) vertices, \(\operatorname{tw}(P_n)=1\) while \(\operatorname{td}(P_n)=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\). Hence bounded treedepth implies bounded treewidth, whereas bounded treewidth does not imply bounded treedepth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treedepth always dominates treewidth plus one, but paths with at least two vertices have constant treewidth and logarithmically growing treedepth.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a nonempty finite undirected graph.
Treedepth counts the number of vertices on a longest root-to-leaf chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tw}(G)+1\leq\operatorname{td}(G)\), and paths separate the two parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Width Without Numeric Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dual-graph width alone to control binary integer-program feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider feasibility systems \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i x_i=b\) with \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) and binary-encoded positive integers \(a_i,b\). Their dual constraint graph has one vertex, hence treewidth zero and treedepth one. Feasibility is nevertheless the SUBSET-SUM decision problem and is NP-complete. Thus bounded dual treewidth or dual treedepth, without a bound on coefficient magnitudes or another numeric parameter, does not yield polynomial-time solvability unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single binary-encoded equality has minimal dual width but already expresses NP-complete SUBSET-SUM, so structural width alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: Coefficients and the right-hand side are encoded in binary.
The dual graph has one vertex per constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded dual width alone does not imply polynomial-time integer-program feasibility unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-constraint SUBSET-SUM construction correctly demonstrates the stated failure boundary, and the content kind fits, but the NP-completeness claim and reduction have no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Dependence Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic para-NP-hardness boundary for algorithms parameterized by structural width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a parameterized decision problem with parameter \(k\). If some fixed value \(k_0\) yields an NP-hard slice \(\{I:(I,k_0)\in\Pi\}\), then, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no algorithm decides every instance in time \(f(k)\,|I|^c\) for any computable function \(f\) and constant \(c\). Indeed, fixing \(k=k_0\) would make the NP-hard slice polynomial-time decidable. Such a fixed slice therefore rules out fixed-parameter tractability with respect to \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP-hard constant-parameter slice excludes every fixed-parameter running time in that parameter unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(k_0\) is independent of the input size.
The slice at \(k_0\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no running time \(f(k)|I|^c\) decides \(\Pi\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-parameter-slice argument correctly excludes an FPT running time unless P=NP, and complexity_bound fits the terminal container, but no authoritative locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Structure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary caused by allowing a structural-width bound to vary without a uniform global bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite graph \(G\) has finite treewidth and finite treedepth. Consequently, \(\bigcup_{k\geq0}\{G:\operatorname{tw}(G)\leq k\}\) and \(\bigcup_{k\geq1}\{G:\operatorname{td}(G)\leq k\}\) both equal the class of all finite graphs. Therefore an algorithmic claim assuming only an instance-dependent finite width, with no uniform bound or explicit parameter dependence, imposes no structural restriction and cannot inherit a bounded-width complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merely requiring each instance to have some finite width is vacuous because every finite graph satisfies that requirement.
assumptions_latex: Instances have finite associated graphs.
No common width bound is imposed over the instance class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instance-dependent finiteness of treewidth or treedepth alone yields no bounded-width algorithmic regime.

notation.meaning: finite structure graph of an instance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unions over all finite width bounds are correctly identified with all finite graphs, and the failure-boundary role fits. The record nevertheless lacks an inspectable source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Diophantine Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer solution set of a linear equality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), the associated linear Diophantine system is \(Ax=b\) with unknown \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\). It is feasible exactly when \(b\in A\mathbb Z^n\). If \(x_0\) is one integer solution, then every integer solution and no other vector has the form \(x=x_0+z\), where \(z\in\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear Diophantine system seeks integer solutions to integer linear equations; when feasible, its solutions form a lattice coset.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is empty or equals \(x_0+(\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hermite Normal-Form Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-Hermite transformation used as an integer-feasibility interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), a column Hermite normal-form computation produces a unimodular matrix \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) and \(H=AU\) in the selected column-Hermite convention. Because \(U\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb Z^n\), the systems \(Ax=b\) and \(Hz=b\) are equivalent under \(x=Uz\). Thus feasibility, a particular solution, and a basis for the homogeneous integer kernel may be recovered in the transformed coordinates without changing the underlying column lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unimodular column transformation puts the matrix in Hermite form while preserving and explicitly translating all integer solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\).
\(U\) is unimodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\) has an integer solution if and only if \(Hz=b\) does, with \(x=Uz\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smith Normal-Form Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smith decomposition and its divisibility test for integer solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) of rank \(r\), there exist unimodular matrices \(U\in\mathbb Z^{m\times m}\) and \(V\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) such that \(UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0,\ldots)\), where \(d_i>0\) and \(d_i\mid d_{i+1}\). Writing \(c=Ub\), the system \(Ax=b\) is integer-feasible exactly when \(d_i\mid c_i\) for \(1\leq i\leq r\) and \(c_i=0\) for \(i>r\); solutions correspond through \(x=Vy\) and \(Dy=c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smith form diagonalizes an integer system unimodularly, reducing feasibility to divisibility and zero-row tests.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and \(r=\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integer feasibility is equivalent to the displayed divisibility and trailing-zero conditions on \(Ub\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time reduction of a rational lattice basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean specialization producing a basis for the full-rank lattice generated by a nonsingular rational matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}\), there is a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\) of the lattice \(\Lambda=A\mathbb{Z}^n\) such that, for the Euclidean norm \(\|x\|_2:=\sqrt{x^\top x}\), \[\prod_{i=1}^n\|b_i\|_2\leq 2^{n(n-1)/4}|\det A|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a nonsingular rational basis matrix A, a polynomial-time algorithm finds a basis of its lattice whose product of Euclidean lengths is at most 2 to the n(n−1)/4 times the absolute determinant of A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Basis Search for a Solution of (5.1)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depends on the previously defined problem (5.1), matrices C^1 and C^2, and set B^n. Step 2 writes L(C) after Step 1 introduces L(C^1); it is interpreted as the current lattice construction. Failure of both searches is not an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the lattice \(L(C^1)\) and compute a reduced basis. If it contains a column \(\binom{\pm x^1}{0}\) with \(x^1\in B^n\), return \(x^1\), which solves (5.1). Otherwise repeat the procedure with \(C^2\). If a vector \(x^2\in B^n\) is found, return \(1-x^2\), which solves (5.1); otherwise terminate without finding a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduce the lattice constructed from C1 and inspect its basis for the prescribed column form. Such a column yields a solution of (5.1). If it is absent, repeat with C2; a vector found there yields the complementary solution. If neither search succeeds, the algorithm reports only that no solution was found.
assumptions_latex: C^1\text{ and }C^2\text{ are the previously defined constructions for problem (5.1)}
B^n\text{ and the required reduced-basis procedure are defined in the surrounding context}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^1\text{ solves (5.1), or }1-x^2\text{ solves (5.1); otherwise the procedure terminates without finding a solution}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle-polynomial basis reduction for an oracle-specified norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Produces a lattice basis satisfying determinant, approximate-shortest-vector, and basis-product bounds for a norm accessed through a weak norm oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb Q^n$ be linearly independent, let $L=L(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$, and let $N$ be a norm on $\mathbb R^n$ specified by a weak norm oracle and rational numbers $r,R>0$ such that $r\lVert x\rVert_2\le N(x)\le R\lVert x\rVert_2$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^n$. There is an oracle-polynomial-time algorithm producing a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ of $L$ such that
\[
N(b_1)\le 2^{(n-1)/4}C_N^{1/n}(n+1)(\det L)^{1/n},
\]
\[
N(b_1)\le 2^{(n-1)/2}(n+1)\min\{N(b):b\in L,\ b\ne0\},
\]
and
\[
\prod_{i=1}^nN(b_i)\le(n+1)^n2^{n(n-1)/4}C_N\det L,
\]
where $C_N$ is the ratio of the volume of the Euclidean unit ball to the volume of the $N$-unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-rank rational lattice and a weak-oracle norm with rational Euclidean comparison bounds, an oracle-polynomial-time algorithm finds a lattice basis satisfying the stated determinant, approximate-shortest-vector, and product bounds.
assumptions_latex: a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb Q^n\text{ are linearly independent}
L=L(a_1,\ldots,a_n)
N\text{ is a norm on }\mathbb R^n\text{ specified by a weak norm oracle}
r,R\in\mathbb Q_{>0}
r\lVert x\rVert_2\le N(x)\le R\lVert x\rVert_2\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R^n
C_N=\operatorname{vol}(B_2)/\operatorname{vol}(B_N)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ an oracle-polynomial-time algorithm producing a basis }(b_i)_{i=1}^n\text{ satisfying the three stated bounds}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-basis algorithm for a full-dimensional lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative closest-integer size reduction and adjacent-vector swapping using Gram–Schmidt data and the three-quarters condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a basis \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\) of a full-dimensional lattice \(L\), compute its Gram–Schmidt vectors and \(\alpha_{ij}=\langle b_i^*,b_j\rangle/\|b_i^*\|^2\). For \(j=2,\ldots,n\) and \(i=j-1,\ldots,1\), replace \(b_j\) by \(b_j-\widehat{\alpha}_{ij}b_i\), where \(\widehat{\alpha}_{ij}\) is an integer closest to \(\alpha_{ij}\). If some \(j\) satisfies \[\|b_{j+1}^*+\alpha_{j,j+1}b_j^*\|^2<\tfrac34\|b_j^*\|^2,\] interchange \(b_j\) and \(b_{j+1}\), recompute the Gram–Schmidt data, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a full-dimensional lattice basis, size-reduce later vectors by closest-integer multiples of earlier vectors. Swap any adjacent pair violating the three-quarters condition, recompute the orthogonalization, and repeat.
assumptions_latex: L\text{ is a full-dimensional lattice}
B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\text{ is a basis of }L
\alpha_{ij}=\frac{\langle b_i^*,b_j\rangle}{\|b_i^*\|^2}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b_j\leftarrow b_j-\widehat{\alpha}_{ij}b_i\text{ for size reduction, and }(b_j,b_{j+1})\leftarrow(b_{j+1},b_j)\text{ whenever }\|b_{j+1}^*+\alpha_{j,j+1}b_j^*\|^2<\tfrac34\|b_j^*\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced lattice basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the stated Lovász parameter \(3/4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b^1,\ldots,b^n\) be a lattice basis, with Gram--Schmidt vectors \(g^1,\ldots,g^n\) and coefficients \(\mu_{jk}\) given by \(b^j=g^j+\sum_{k<j}\mu_{jk}g^k\). The basis is reduced if \(|\mu_{jk}|\le\tfrac12\) for every \(1\le k<j\le n\), and \(\|g^j+\mu_{j,j-1}g^{j-1}\|^2\ge\tfrac34\|g^{j-1}\|^2\) for every \(2\le j\le n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice basis is reduced when every Gram–Schmidt coefficient has absolute value at most one half and every adjacent pair satisfies the Lovász inequality with parameter three quarters.
assumptions_latex: b^1,\ldots,b^n\text{ is a lattice basis}
b^j=g^j+\sum_{k<j}\mu_{jk}g^k\text{ is its Gram--Schmidt decomposition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall 1\le k<j\le n,\ |\mu_{jk}|\le\tfrac12\right)\land\left(\forall 2\le j\le n,\ \|g^j+\mu_{j,j-1}g^{j-1}\|^2\ge\tfrac34\|g^{j-1}\|^2\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász lattice-basis reduction algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterates size reduction and adjacent swaps for a rational full-rank lattice basis until the stated reduction conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational lattice basis \(B=(b^1,\ldots,b^n)\), repeatedly perform: (1) for \(j=2,\ldots,n\) and \(k=j-1,\ldots,1\), replace \(b^j\leftarrow b^j-\lfloor\mu_{jk}\rceil b^k\), where \(\lfloor a\rceil\) is a closest integer to \(a\); (2) if \(\|g^j+\mu_{j,j-1}g^{j-1}\|^2\ge\tfrac34\|g^{j-1}\|^2\) holds for all \(2\le j\le n\), stop and output \(B\); otherwise choose a violating \(j\), interchange \(b^{j-1}\) and \(b^j\), and repeat. The output is a reduced basis of the same lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a rational lattice basis, size-reduce its Gram–Schmidt coefficients by subtracting closest-integer multiples of earlier vectors. Swap an adjacent pair violating the Lovász inequality and repeat; when no violation remains, output the reduced basis of the original lattice.
assumptions_latex: B=(b^1,\ldots,b^n)\text{ is a rational basis of a full-rank lattice }\Lambda
\lfloor a\rceil\text{ denotes a closest integer to }a
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm outputs a reduced basis }B'\text{ satisfying }B'\mathbb Z^n=\Lambda.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Basis with Bounded Length Product
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent existence guarantee for full-rank Euclidean lattice bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every lattice $L\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, there exists a basis $(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ of $L$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^n\|b_i\|\le c_n\det L$, where $c_n$ depends only on $n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lattice in dimension n has a basis whose product of vector lengths is at most a dimension-dependent constant times the lattice determinant.
assumptions_latex: L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a lattice}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a basis }(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\text{ of }L:\ \prod_{i=1}^n\|b_i\|\le c_n\det L,\quad c_n=c(n).

knowledge_statements.title: LLL Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical rational-basis LLL algorithm with fixed Lovász parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\) and fix \(\delta\in(1/4,1)\). Compute Gram–Schmidt vectors \(b_i^*\) and coefficients \(\mu_{i,j}\). Repeatedly size-reduce by replacing \(b_k\) with \(b_k-\lfloor\mu_{k,j}\rceil b_j\) for \(j<k\). If \(\delta\lVert b_{k-1}^*\rVert^2>\lVert b_k^*+\mu_{k,k-1}b_{k-1}^*\rVert^2\), swap \(b_{k-1},b_k\), update the Gram–Schmidt data, and continue. Stop when all size-reduction and Lovász conditions hold; output the resulting basis of the same lattice. For fixed \(\delta\), the bit complexity is polynomial in the encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LLL alternates integer size reductions and Lovász-triggered swaps, terminating in polynomial time with a reduced basis of the same lattice.
assumptions_latex: The input vectors are linearly independent and rational.
\(1/4<\delta<1\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced basis generating the input lattice.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic description, Lovász test, lattice preservation, and fixed-parameter polynomial bit-complexity claim are standard and consistent, but no authoritative algorithm or complexity locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LLL-Reduced Basis with Parameter Three Quarters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size-reduction and Lovász conditions for the standard LLL reduction parameter; the accompanying parameter remark records the stated polynomiality boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ be an ordered basis of a lattice $L$, let $(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)$ be its Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization, and let $b_j=\sum_{i\le j}\mu_{ji}b_i^*$. The basis is reduced if $|\mu_{ji}|\le\tfrac12$ for every $1\le i<j\le n$ and $\|b_{j+1}^*+\mu_{j+1,j}b_j^*\|^2\ge\tfrac34\|b_j^*\|^2$ for every $j=1,\ldots,n-1$. The factor $\tfrac34$ may be replaced by a fixed value in $(\tfrac14,1)$; for the value $1$, the source does not guarantee polynomiality of the resulting algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordered lattice basis is reduced when its Gram–Schmidt coefficients are size-reduced and adjacent vectors satisfy the Lovász condition with parameter 3/4. A fixed parameter strictly between 1/4 and 1 may be used, while parameter 1 lacks the stated polynomiality guarantee.
assumptions_latex: L\text{ is a lattice}
(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\text{ is an ordered basis of }L
b_j=\sum_{i\le j}\mu_{ji}b_i^*\text{ for its Gram\text{--}Schmidt vectors }b_i^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (b_1,\ldots,b_n)\text{ is reduced}\iff\left[|\mu_{ji}|\le\tfrac12\ \forall i<j\right]\land\left[\|b_{j+1}^*+\mu_{j+1,j}b_j^*\|^2\ge\tfrac34\|b_j^*\|^2\ \forall j<n\right].

children.title: Primal Lattice Reduction
children.top_down_role: Basis reduction viewed in the original lattice.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Lattice Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LLL reduction applied directly to a primal lattice basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a full-column-rank rational matrix \(B=[b_1\ \cdots\ b_n]\) generating the lattice \(L=B\mathbb Z^n\), apply the LLL algorithm with fixed \(\delta\in(1/4,1)\) to its columns. The algorithm returns a unimodular matrix \(U\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\) and the reduced basis \(B'=BU\). Since \(U\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb Z^n\), one has \(B'\mathbb Z^n=L\). Stop when the columns of \(B'\) satisfy size reduction and the Lovász inequalities; output \(B'\) as the primal reduced basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal reduction applies LLL to the given lattice basis and preserves the lattice through a unimodular coordinate change.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) has full column rank and rational entries.
\(1/4<\delta<1\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B'=BU\) is \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced and generates the same primal lattice.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Applying LLL to the primal basis and recording its unimodular basis transformation is mathematically coherent and algorithmically appropriate, but the record has no source.

children.title: Dual Lattice Reduction
children.top_down_role: Basis reduction viewed in the dual lattice.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Lattice Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LLL reduction performed on the dual basis of a full-rank lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonsingular rational basis matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) for \(L=B\mathbb Z^n\), form the dual basis \(B^{-T}\), which generates \(L^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:y^Tx\in\mathbb Z\text{ for every }x\in L\}\). Apply LLL with fixed \(\delta\in(1/4,1)\) to the columns of \(B^{-T}\). On termination, output \(B^*=B^{-T}V\), where \(V\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\); then \(B^*\mathbb Z^n=L^*\) and \(B^*\) is \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual reduction constructs the dual basis, applies LLL there, and preserves the dual lattice by a unimodular transformation.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular.
\(1/4<\delta<1\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(B^*=B^{-T}V\) is a reduced basis of \(L^*\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a full-rank square basis, the stated dual lattice, dual basis, and unimodular LLL transformation are correct. An authoritative locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis and Gram–Schmidt Structure Produced by Procedure 27.16
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Procedure-specific basis property in the dual-lattice construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If Procedure 27.16 outputs \(\mathbf w_1,\ldots,\mathbf w_n\), then \(\mathbf w_n,\mathbf w_{n-1},\ldots,\mathbf w_1\) is a basis of \(\mathcal L\) with Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization \(\left(\frac{\mathbf v_n}{\|\mathbf v_n\|^2},\ldots,\frac{\mathbf v_1}{\|\mathbf v_1\|^2}\right)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vectors output by Procedure 27.16, in reverse order, form a basis of the lattice, and their Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization is the reversed sequence of vectors v_i divided by their squared norms.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf w_1,\ldots,\mathbf w_n\text{ are the vectors output by Procedure 27.16}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathbf w_n,\ldots,\mathbf w_1)\text{ is a basis of }\mathcal L\text{ with Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization }\left(\frac{\mathbf v_n}{\|\mathbf v_n\|^2},\ldots,\frac{\mathbf v_1}{\|\mathbf v_1\|^2}\right)\).

children.title: Primal–Dual Quality Transfer
children.top_down_role: Relationships between reduction quality in primal and dual bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Quality Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean successive-minima transference between a lattice and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a full-rank lattice, let \(L^*\) be its dual, and let \(\lambda_i(L)\) denote the \(i\)-th Euclidean successive minimum. For every \(1\leq i\leq n\), transference gives \(1\leq\lambda_i(L)\lambda_{n-i+1}(L^*)\leq n\). Consequently, an upper or lower bound on a primal successive minimum transfers, with dimension-dependent loss, to the complementary dual successive minimum, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary successive minima of a lattice and its dual have product between one and the dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(L\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
Successive minima use the Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\leq\lambda_i(L)\lambda_{n-i+1}(L^*)\leq n\) for every \(i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complementary successive-minima transference inequality is a nontrivial theorem and the duality content kind fits, but it cannot be accepted without a specific authoritative theorem or page locator.

children.title: Duality-Sensitive Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where guarantees fail to transfer cleanly across lattice duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Sensitive Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided shortest-vector control need not control the dual shortest vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t\geq1\), let \(L_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t,\ldots,t)\mathbb Z^n\). Then \(\lambda_1(L_t)=1\), while \(L_t^*=\operatorname{diag}(1,t^{-1},\ldots,t^{-1})\mathbb Z^n\) and \(\lambda_1(L_t^*)=t^{-1}\). Thus a uniform primal bound on \(\lambda_1(L)\) alone gives no positive dimension-only lower bound on \(\lambda_1(L^*)\). Primal–dual transfer must instead use complementary minima, determinant information, or another scale-sensitive hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice family can keep its primal shortest length fixed while its dual shortest length tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq2\) and \(t\geq1\).
Lengths are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Control of \(\lambda_1(L)\) alone does not control \(\lambda_1(L^*)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal lattice family correctly shows that fixed primal shortest-vector length does not provide a positive dimension-only lower bound for the dual shortest-vector length. The failure-boundary kind fits, but no source is cited.

children.title: Shortest-Vector Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Vector Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact shortest-vector oracle for a full-rank rational lattice under an explicitly supplied norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a full-column-rank matrix \(B\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) on \(\mathbb{R}^m\). Form the lattice \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}\). The shortest-vector interface returns a vector \(v\in L(B)\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \[\lVert v\rVert=\lambda_1(L(B)):=\min\{\lVert Bz\rVert:z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\}.\] Equivalently, it may return a coefficient vector \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \(v=Bz\). The interface terminates only with such an exact minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a lattice basis and norm, return a nonzero lattice vector of minimum norm, optionally through its integer coefficient vector.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) has column rank \(n\).
\(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) is a norm whose values can be compared exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in L(B)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\lVert v\rVert=\lambda_1(L(B))\).

notation.meaning: Lattice generated by the columns of B.
Length of a shortest nonzero vector of L.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact SVP interface is mathematically coherent and the algorithm kind fits the leaf, but no cited source supports the norm model or exact-output specification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Integer Search Produces a Shortest Lattice Vector
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a shortest vector through a bounded integer-coefficient problem relative to a chosen lattice basis; \(\alpha(B)\) retains the source's notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional lattice, let \(B\) be a basis of \(L\), and let \(x^0\) solve \(\min\{\|Bx\|:x\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},\ |x_j|\le \alpha(B)/|\det B|\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,n\}\). Then \(v=Bx^0\) is a shortest vector in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional lattice, minimizing the norm of a basis-generated vector over nonzero integer coefficients within the stated coordinate bounds produces a shortest lattice vector.
assumptions_latex: L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a full-dimensional lattice}
B\text{ is a basis of }L
x^0\in\arg\min\left\{\|Bx\|:x\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},\ |x_j|\le\frac{\alpha(B)}{|\det B|}\ \forall j\right\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bx^0\in\arg\min\{\|v\|:v\in L\setminus\{0\}\}

children.title: Approximate Vector Oracles
children.top_down_role: Approximate access models for short-vector or nearby-vector tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Vector Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative approximation interfaces for shortest-vector and closest-vector lattice queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an approximation factor \(\gamma\geq1\), a \(\gamma\)-SVP oracle maps a lattice basis \(B\) to a nonzero \(v\in L(B)\) satisfying \(\lVert v\rVert\leq\gamma\lambda_1(L(B))\). A \(\gamma\)-CVP oracle maps \((B,t)\) to \(v\in L(B)\) satisfying \(\lVert t-v\rVert\leq\gamma\operatorname{dist}(t,L(B))\). The guarantee is multiplicative in the chosen norm. For CVP instances with \(t\in L(B)\), the zero optimum forces every valid approximate oracle to return \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor-gamma vector oracle returns an SVP or CVP solution whose norm or target distance is at most gamma times optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma\geq1\).
\(B\) is a basis of a full-rank lattice in its linear span.
The same norm defines both the optimum and approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert v\rVert\leq\gamma\lambda_1(L(B))\) for SVP, or \(\lVert t-v\rVert\leq\gamma\operatorname{dist}(t,L(B))\) for CVP.

notation.meaning: Distance from the target to the lattice.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicative SVP and CVP definitions are precise, including the zero-optimum CVP case, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Vector-Oracle Complexity Transfer
children.top_down_role: Complexity transfers from lattice vector subroutines to integer-programming routines.

knowledge_statements.title: Vector-Oracle Complexity Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition bound for integer-programming reductions that invoke lattice-vector oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an algorithm on an input of bit length \(L\) that performs at most \(q(n,L)\) vector-oracle calls and otherwise uses at most \(P(n,L)\) bit operations. If call \(j\) has encoded length at most \(S(n,L)\) and the selected oracle runs in time \(T_{\mathrm{vec}}(n,s)\) on length \(s\), then the composed running time satisfies \[T_{\mathrm{total}}(n,L)\leq P(n,L)+q(n,L)T_{\mathrm{vec}}(n,S(n,L)).\] Thus polynomial bounds for \(P\), \(q\), \(S\), and \(T_{\mathrm{vec}}\) transfer polynomial-time solvability to the composed reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle calls transfer their running time additively: boundedly many polynomial-size vector queries preserve polynomial time when the oracle and remaining work are polynomial.
assumptions_latex: Every oracle query has encoded length at most \(S(n,L)\).
The reduction makes at most \(q(n,L)\) oracle calls.
Oracle construction and all non-oracle work cost at most \(P(n,L)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{total}}(n,L)\leq P(n,L)+q(n,L)T_{\mathrm{vec}}(n,S(n,L))\).

notation.meaning: Bit length of the original input.
Vector-oracle running time on encoded length s.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composition principle fits the complexity-bound leaf, but the displayed bound requires T_vec(n,s) to be nondecreasing in s or to denote a worst-case supremum over lengths at most s. No supporting source is supplied.

children.title: Rounding-Width Transference Calculus
children.top_down_role: Geometric infrastructure connecting convex bodies with lattice directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: John-type rounding of a full-dimensional convex body by a contained ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact, convex set with nonempty interior. There exist \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and a nonsingular linear map \(A\) such that, for the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2^n\), \[c+A B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq c+nA B_2^n.\] The ellipsoid \(E=c+A B_2^n\) is an \(n\)-rounding of \(K\). If \(K\) is centrally symmetric about \(c\), the sharper containment \(K\subseteq c+\sqrt n A B_2^n\) can be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every full-dimensional compact convex body contains an ellipsoid whose dilation by n covers it; the symmetric case admits factor square-root n.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and convex.
\(\operatorname{int}(K)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c+A B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq c+nA B_2^n\), with factor \(\sqrt n\) when \(K\) is centrally symmetric.

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball in n dimensions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The John-type containment and symmetric improvement are standard, but the existential result is theorem-like rather than merely a representation. No authoritative locator supports the constants or role selection.

children.title: Lattice Width
children.top_down_role: Width of a convex region relative to integral lattice directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum directional width over nonzero vectors of the dual lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and bounded, and let \(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a full-rank lattice with dual \(L^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:y^Tx\in\mathbb{Z}\text{ for all }x\in L\}\). For \(y\in L^*\setminus\{0\}\), define \(w_y(K)=\sup_{x\in K}y^Tx-\inf_{x\in K}y^Tx\). The lattice width of \(K\) relative to \(L\) is \[w_L(K)=\inf_{y\in L^*\setminus\{0\}}w_y(K).\] For compact \(K\), the extrema exist; for full-dimensional compact convex \(K\), the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lattice width is the smallest range of a bounded set when projected along any nonzero dual-lattice direction.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and bounded.
\(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_L(K)=\inf_{0\neq y\in L^*}\left(\sup_{x\in K}y^Tx-\inf_{x\in K}y^Tx\right)\).

notation.meaning: Width of K in direction y.
Lattice width of K relative to L.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and attainment claim are mathematically consistent for the stated compact full-dimensional case, but neither is supported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Flat Direction Selection
children.top_down_role: Identification of lattice directions exhibiting small directional width.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Direction Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of a dual-lattice direction attaining minimum lattice width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a full-dimensional compact convex body \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and a full-rank lattice \(L\). Search over primitive vectors \(y\in L^*\setminus\{0\}\), evaluating \(w_y(K)=\max_{x\in K}y^Tx-\min_{x\in K}y^Tx\), and output any minimizer \[y^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\neq y\in L^*}w_y(K).\] The selected flat direction satisfies \(w_{y^*}(K)=w_L(K)\). Primitivity may be imposed because replacing \(y=ku\), with integer \(k\geq2\), by \(u\in L^*\) divides the width by \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a primitive nonzero dual-lattice vector minimizing directional width; its width equals the lattice width of the body.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact, convex, and full-dimensional.
\(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
Directional maxima and minima can be evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^*\in L^*\setminus\{0\}\) is primitive and \(w_{y^*}(K)=w_L(K)\).

notation.meaning: Directional width of K along y.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A minimum-width primitive direction exists under the assumptions, but searching an infinite set does not specify a terminating algorithm or complexity model. A source-backed finite procedure or explicit oracle interface is required.

children.title: Width-Certificate Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity of representing or obtaining useful width witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Width-Certificate Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time verification of a supplied rational width direction for a rational polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) be a nonempty bounded rational polytope and let \(y\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\) be supplied in binary. Its directional width is computed by the two linear programs \[\beta=\max\{y^Tx:Ax\leq b\},\qquad \alpha=\min\{y^Tx:Ax\leq b\},\qquad w_y(P)=\beta-\alpha.\] Primal optimal solutions together with feasible dual multipliers proving both objective bounds form a certificate verifiable in time polynomial in the combined encoding length of \(A,b,y\), and the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rational polytope and supplied integer direction, two linear-programming optimality certificates verify the directional width in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are rational and binary encoded.
\(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\) is nonempty and bounded.
\(y\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\) is binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The claimed value \(w_y(P)=\beta-\alpha\) has a polynomial-time verifiable rational certificate.

notation.meaning: Minimum and maximum of the directional linear functional.
Width of P in direction y.

children.title: Dimension-Reduction Consequences
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional structure exposed by sufficiently narrow lattice directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Reduction Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching on integral hyperplanes orthogonal to a dual-lattice direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact, let \(L\) be a full-rank lattice, and choose \(y\in L^*\setminus\{0\}\). Put \(\alpha=\min_{x\in K}y^Tx\) and \(\beta=\max_{x\in K}y^Tx\). Every point of \(K\cap L\) lies in one of the affine slices \[K\cap\{x:y^Tx=k\},\qquad k=\lceil\alpha\rceil,\ldots,\lfloor\beta\rfloor.\] Hence at most \(\max\{0,\lfloor\beta\rfloor-\lceil\alpha\rceil+1\}\leq\lfloor w_y(K)\rfloor+1\) slices need examination, and each nonempty slice is contained in an affine space of dimension at most \(n-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-lattice direction partitions all lattice points of a compact set among at most floor(width)+1 lower-dimensional integral hyperplane slices.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact.
\(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
\(y\in L^*\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\cap L\) is covered by at most \(\lfloor w_y(K)\rfloor+1\) affine slices of dimension at most \(n-1\).

notation.meaning: Minimum and maximum projection values on K.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The slice covering, count, and dimension conclusion are correct under the stated assumptions and fit a theorem leaf, but no source locator is supplied.

children.title: Primal Successive Minima
children.top_down_role: Successive-minimum parameters associated with a primal lattice and convex body.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Successive Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive minima of an origin-symmetric convex body with respect to a full-rank lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact, convex, origin-symmetric, and full-dimensional, and let \(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a full-rank lattice. For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the \(i\)-th primal successive minimum is \[\lambda_i(K,L)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\dim\operatorname{span}(L\cap\lambda K)\geq i\}.\] Thus \(\lambda_i(K,L)\) is the least dilation factor at which \(\lambda K\) contains \(i\) linearly independent lattice vectors. The sequence is finite and satisfies \(0<\lambda_1(K,L)\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n(K,L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The i-th successive minimum is the smallest dilation of a symmetric convex body containing i linearly independent lattice vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact, convex, origin-symmetric, and full-dimensional.
\(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
\(1\leq i\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_i(K,L)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\dim\operatorname{span}(L\cap\lambda K)\geq i\}\).

notation.meaning: Dilation of K by factor lambda about the origin.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal successive-minima definition is precise and correctly classified, but it lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Dual Successive Minima
children.top_down_role: Successive-minimum parameters associated with the corresponding dual objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Successive Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive minima of the polar body with respect to the dual lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an origin-symmetric full-dimensional convex body \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define its polar by \(K^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:y^Tx\leq1\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). For a full-rank lattice \(L\), let \(L^*=\{y:y^Tx\in\mathbb{Z}\text{ for every }x\in L\}\). The \(i\)-th dual successive minimum is \[\lambda_i(K^*,L^*)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\dim\operatorname{span}(L^*\cap\lambda K^*)\geq i\}.\] It measures the dilation needed to obtain \(i\) linearly independent dual-lattice directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual successive minima are the successive minima of the polar body measured against the dual lattice.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact, convex, origin-symmetric, and full-dimensional.
\(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
\(1\leq i\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_i(K^*,L^*)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\dim\operatorname{span}(L^*\cap\lambda K^*)\geq i\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polar body, dual lattice, and dual successive minimum are consistently defined, but no supporting source locator is supplied.

children.title: Transference Relations
children.top_down_role: Quantitative links between primal and dual lattice parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Transference Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical polar-body transference bounds for paired primal and dual successive minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact, convex, origin-symmetric, and full-dimensional, and let \(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a full-rank lattice. For every \(i\in\{1,ldots,n\}\), the paired successive minima of \((K,L)\) and \((K^*,L^*)\) satisfy \[1\leq\lambda_i(K,L)\lambda_{n-i+1}(K^*,L^*)\leq n!.\] In the Euclidean specialization \(K=B_2^n\), the upper bound improves to \(n\). Thus a small primal minimum forces the complementary dual minimum to be large enough, while the product remains dimension-bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary primal and dual successive minima have product between one and a dimension-dependent constant; the Euclidean upper bound is n.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact, convex, origin-symmetric, and full-dimensional.
\(L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
\(1\leq i\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\leq\lambda_i(K,L)\lambda_{n-i+1}(K^*,L^*)\leq n!\), and the upper bound is \(n\) when \(K=B_2^n\).

notation.meaning: The i-th successive minimum for the displayed body-lattice pair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact general and Euclidean transference constants require authoritative confirmation. Moreover, the index set contains the literal text 'ldots' instead of the LaTeX command \ldots, so the quantified domain is malformed.

children.title: Approximation-Quality Consequences
children.top_down_role: Effects of approximate minima information on geometric lattice routines.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Quality Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative consequences of successive-minima transference for symmetric convex bodies and full-rank lattices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a centrally symmetric convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\), and let \(\Lambda\) be a full-rank lattice. For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), transference gives \[1\le \lambda_i(K,\Lambda)\lambda_{n+1-i}(K^\circ,\Lambda^*)\le n.\] Consequently, any bounds \(L\le\lambda_{n+1-i}(K^\circ,\Lambda^*)\le U\) imply \(1/U\le\lambda_i(K,\Lambda)\le n/L\). Thus an \(\alpha\)-factor estimate of the relevant dual minimum transfers to an \(n\alpha\)-factor enclosure of the primal minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative estimate of a dual successive minimum yields, through transference, a primal estimate whose additional worst-case loss is at most the dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is centrally symmetric, convex, compact, and has \(0\) in its interior.
\(\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a full-rank lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le\lambda_{n+1-i}(K^\circ,\Lambda^*)\le U\Longrightarrow 1/U\le\lambda_i(K,\Lambda)\le n/L\).

notation.meaning: The i-th successive minimum of K with respect to Lambda.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive reduction by slicing a convex integer-feasibility instance along an integral width direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a convex set \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) and a primitive vector \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\). Compute \(\ell=\inf_{x\in K}a^\top x\) and \(u=\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x\). For every integer \(k\in[\lceil\ell\rceil,\lfloor u\rfloor]\), solve recursively on the affine lattice \(H_k\cap\mathbb Z^n\), where \(H_k=\{x:a^\top x=k\}\). Return a discovered lattice point; return infeasible if every slice is infeasible. Each nonempty slice has lattice dimension \(n-1\), and the number of recursive subproblems is at most \(\lfloor u\rfloor-\lceil\ell\rceil+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on every integral level intersecting the convex set. Each branch is an integer-feasibility problem in one lower lattice dimension.
assumptions_latex: Extrema in direction \(a\) can be computed or bounded.
\(a\) is primitive, so every nonempty integral level has the expected affine lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\cap\mathbb Z^n=\bigcup_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{\lfloor u\rfloor}(K\cap H_k\cap\mathbb Z^n)\), with each branch of lattice dimension \(n-1\).

notation.meaning: Affine hyperplane at integral level k of the branching direction.
Lower and upper support values of K in direction a.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Body Flatness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric flatness theorem for lattice-point-free convex bodies in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(n\ge1\), there exists a finite constant \(F(n)\) such that every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(K\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\) has lattice width \[w(K)=\min_{a\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\left(\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x-\inf_{x\in K}a^\top x\right)\le F(n).\] Equivalently, some nonzero integral direction has bounded width depending only on the dimension, not on the location, diameter, or description of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lattice-point-free convex body has a nonzero integral direction whose width is bounded solely as a function of dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a convex body.
\(K\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(K)\le F(n)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Lattice width of K with respect to the integer lattice.

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Flatness

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Flatness
children.top_down_role: Effects of body representation on access to flatness information.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Flatness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of the representation-invariant width bound from representation-dependent algorithmic access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two valid encodings describe the same convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\). Its lattice width \(w(K)\) and the implication \(K\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\Rightarrow w(K)\le F(n)\) are invariant under the encoding. In contrast, an algorithmic flatness oracle must compute or approximate support values \(h_K(a)=\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x\) and produce a suitable integral direction. Polynomial running time therefore requires an explicit access model, such as rational inequalities with bounded bit length or polynomial-time separation and optimization oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flatness is geometric and encoding-independent, but finding a flat direction efficiently depends on how the convex set is represented and accessed.
assumptions_latex: Both encodings define the same convex body \(K\).
The algorithm receives a specified finite encoding or oracle-access model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(K)\) is representation-invariant, while the complexity of computing a witnessing direction need not be.

notation.meaning: Support function of K in direction a.

children.title: Convex-to-Polyhedral Transfer

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-to-Polyhedral Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of convex-body flatness from outer polyhedral approximations of compact lattice-point-free bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact, convex, and disjoint from \(\mathbb Z^n\). Because \(K\) has positive distance from the discrete lattice, there exists a bounded polytope \(P\) with \(K\subseteq P\) and \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\). Monotonicity of directional width yields \(w(K)\le w(P)\). Hence any uniform polyhedral flatness bound \(w(P)\le B(n)\) transfers to \(w(K)\le B(n)\). Conversely, polytopes are convex bodies, so the optimal constants for the two bounded full-dimensional classes coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact lattice-free convex body admits a lattice-free outer polytope; width monotonicity transfers every uniform polyhedral bound back to the body.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is compact, convex, full-dimensional, and lattice-point-free.
The polyhedral bound is uniform over bounded full-dimensional lattice-point-free polytopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{conv}}(n)=F_{\mathrm{poly}}(n)\).

notation.meaning: Optimal flatness constant over convex bodies.
Optimal flatness constant over bounded polytopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Flatness Constant Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal flatness constants indexed by dimension and, optionally, by a full-rank lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge1\), define the integer-lattice flatness constant by \[F(n)=\sup\{w(K):K\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is a convex body and }K\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\}.\] More generally, for a full-rank lattice \(\Lambda\), define \(F(\Lambda)\) using width \(w_\Lambda(K)=\min_{0\ne y\in\Lambda^*}(\sup_{x\in K}y^\top x-\inf_{x\in K}y^\top x)\) and the condition \(K\cap\Lambda=\varnothing\). Under an invertible linear change sending \(\Lambda\) to \(\mathbb Z^n\), these definitions agree, so \(F(\Lambda)=F(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension-n flatness constant is the supremum lattice width of lattice-point-free convex bodies; the lattice-relative version is invariant under linear normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) ranges over full-dimensional compact convex sets.
\(\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a full-rank lattice in the generalized definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Dimension Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical dimension-growth envelope for the Euclidean flatness constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist universal constants \(c,C>0\) such that, for every sufficiently large \(n\), the flatness constant satisfies \[c n\le F(n)\le C n^{3/2}.\] Thus flatness cannot be bounded independently of dimension, while the classical transference-based upper estimate is polynomial in dimension. The displayed interval is a robust classical envelope and does not assert optimality of the upper exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flatness constant grows at least linearly and admits a classical order-n^{3/2} upper bound, so its dependence on dimension is unavoidable but polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(F(n)\) uses the integer-lattice width normalization for lattice-point-free convex bodies.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Dimension Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational form of any numerically specified upper bound on the flatness constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an explicitly computable function \(B:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \(F(n)\le B(n)\). Every lattice-point-free convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) then admits \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \(w_a(K)\le B(n)\). Branching on the integral levels of \(a^\top x\) creates at most \[\lfloor\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x\rfloor-\lceil\inf_{x\in K}a^\top x\rceil+1\le\lfloor B(n)\rfloor+1\] nonempty candidate slices. Hence a numerical dimension bound immediately gives a numerical branching bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any explicit upper bound on the flatness constant gives an explicit bound—its floor plus one—on the number of integral slices to inspect.

children.title: Runtime Sensitivity to Flatness
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects produced by the size of available flatness bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Sensitivity to Flatness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursion-size dependence of flat-direction branching on the adopted flatness bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a dimension-\(d\) node can find a width direction and prepare all slices in time \(p_d(L)\), and suppose every lattice-point-free node has width at most \(B(d)\). If each slice has encoding length at most \(q_d(L)\), then the worst-case recursion satisfies \[T(d,L)\le(\lfloor B(d)\rfloor+1)T(d-1,q_d(L))+p_d(L).\] When \(p_d,q_d\) are polynomially bounded, the number of leaves is at most \(\prod_{j=1}^d(\lfloor B(j)\rfloor+1)\). Thus improved flatness bounds directly reduce the dimension-dependent factor, while fixed \(d\) preserves polynomial dependence on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flatness controls branching multiplicatively: the recursion has at most the product of one-plus-flatness bounds many leaves, with polynomial overhead in fixed dimension.
assumptions_latex: Direction finding, support optimization, and slice construction have polynomial bit complexity.
Slice encodings have polynomially bounded length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(d,L)\le(\lfloor B(d)\rfloor+1)T(d-1,q_d(L))+p_d(L)\).

notation.meaning: Worst-case runtime in dimension d and encoding length L.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Direction Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-dimension feasibility branching using a flatness witness or a found lattice point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) with an optimization or separation representation. Invoke a flatness subroutine that either returns \(z\in K\cap\mathbb Z^n\) or a primitive \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \(w_a(K)\le B(n)\). In the first case output \(z\). Otherwise compute \(\ell=\inf_{x\in K}a^\top x\) and \(u=\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x\), recursively test every slice \(K\cap\{x:a^\top x=k\}\) for \(k=\lceil\ell\rceil,\ldots,\lfloor u\rfloor\), and output a found lattice point or infeasible. At most \(\lfloor B(n)\rfloor+1\) slices are generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either the flatness routine finds an integer point or supplies a narrow integral direction; the algorithm then recursively searches every intersecting integral slice.
assumptions_latex: The flatness subroutine is correct for the supplied representation.
Support values and affine-lattice parametrizations can be computed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm is correct and branches into at most \(\lfloor B(n)\rfloor+1\) dimension-\(n-1\) subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Flatness Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assumptions under which no dimension-only flatness conclusion or algorithmic guarantee follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity, lattice avoidance, and fixed dimension play distinct roles. If lattice avoidance is removed, the boxes \(K_R=[0,R]^n\) have \(w(K_R)=R\to\infty\). If convexity is removed, the sets \[S_R=[0,R]^n\setminus\bigcup_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}B(z,\varepsilon),\qquad 0<\varepsilon<1/3,\] contain no lattice point but have unbounded directional extent as \(R\to\infty\), so the convex flatness theorem does not apply. Finally, since \(F(n)\) grows with \(n\), fixed-dimension polynomiality derived from flat-direction enumeration does not imply polynomiality when dimension is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flatness can fail without lattice avoidance or convexity, and dimension-dependent branching does not yield polynomial time when dimension varies with the input.
assumptions_latex: Width of a nonconvex set is interpreted by the same support-value formula.
\(R\) tends to infinity while \(n\) is fixed in the first two examples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing the stated hypotheses destroys either the width bound or the fixed-dimension runtime consequence.

notation.meaning: Large convex boxes containing lattice points.
Nonconvex boxes with neighborhoods of lattice points removed.

Mere unbounded directional extent does not by itself establish unbounded minimum lattice width.
