children.title: Ellipsoidal Rounding Interface
children.top_down_role: Rounded convex representations used within fixed-dimensional lattice analysis.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-dimensional convex body.
\(E=c+A B_2^n\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) nonsingular.
\(E\subseteq K\subseteq c+\alpha(E-c)\) for some \(\alpha\geq 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) supplies an inner norm and an outer approximation for \(K\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball in dimension n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the rounding interface used by the geometric Lenstra recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(\alpha\)-ellipsoidal rounding of \(K\) is a pair \((c,A)\) satisfying \[E:=c+A B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq c+\alpha A B_2^n.\] Consequently, membership in the inner ellipsoid is certified by \(\|A^{-1}(x-c)\|_2\leq 1\), while every \(x\in K\) satisfies \(\|A^{-1}(x-c)\|_2\leq\alpha\). Thus the affine map \(y=A^{-1}(x-c)\) places the feasible body between the concentric Euclidean balls \(B_2^n\) and \(\alpha B_2^n\), providing the geometric interface to lattice-point detection or flat-direction branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rounding places the convex body between two concentric ellipsoids whose radii differ by at most a factor alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Rounding Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this particular rounding convention or its claimed Lenstra-interface role.

children.title: Deep Lattice Points
children.top_down_role: Feasible lattice points lying sufficiently far from the rounded body's boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(E=c+A B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(A\) is nonsingular and \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_E(z)\geq\rho\) implies \(z+\rho A B_2^n\subseteq K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses depth relative to the inner rounding ellipsoid, not boundary distance in an arbitrary norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\leq\rho\leq1\), an integer point \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) is \(\rho\)-deep in the rounded body relative to \(E\) when \[\delta_E(z):=1-\|A^{-1}(z-c)\|_2\geq\rho.\] Equivalently, \(z\in c+(1-\rho)A B_2^n\). The triangle inequality then gives \(z+\rho A B_2^n\subseteq E\subseteq K\). In particular, every point with nonnegative ellipsoidal depth is an integer feasible point of \(K\), while positive depth certifies a translated ellipsoidal neighborhood contained in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice point is rho-deep when its ellipsoidal distance from the center is at most one minus rho.
knowledge_statements.title: Deep Lattice Points

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed depth definition and neighborhood implication are coherent, but the terminology and its role in the Lenstra framework are uncited. The sentence invoking the triangle inequality is also proof text and should be removed after sourcing.

children.title: Deep-Point Detection
children.top_down_role: Computational access to the deep-lattice-point regime.

assumptions_latex: \(E=c+A B_2^n\) with \(A\) nonsingular.
An exact closest-vector oracle is available for the lattice \(A^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is \(z^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) minimizing \(\|A^{-1}(z-c)\|_2\), with correct detection of \(\rho\)-deep points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact detection is expressed as a closest-vector computation in the ellipsoidal norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(c\), \(A\), and \(0\leq\rho
egthickspace<1\), form \(L=A^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^n\) and target \(t=A^{-1}c\). Compute \(v^*\in L\) minimizing \(\|v-t\|_2\), and recover the unique associated \(z^*=A v^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n\). If \(\|v^*-t\|_2\leq1-\rho\), output \(z^*\) as a \(\rho\)-deep lattice point; otherwise report that no \(\rho\)-deep lattice point exists in \(E\). Correctness follows from the identity \(\|v-t\|_2=\|A^{-1}(z-c)\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transforming the ellipsoid turns deep-point detection into an exact closest-vector problem for a transformed lattice.
knowledge_statements.title: Deep-Point Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact CVP formulation is plausible and the algorithm kind fits the leaf, but no source establishes this detection subroutine or its computational model. The correctness-derivation sentence is proof text.

children.title: Rounding-Quality Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-Quality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how rounding distortion shifts the boundary between deep and flat cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=c+A B_2^n\) and suppose \(E\subseteq K\subseteq c+\alpha A B_2^n\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(\alpha\geq 1\). For every \(a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\), \[2\lVert A^T a\rVert_2=w_a(E)\leq w_a(K)\leq w_a\bigl(c+\alpha A B_2^n\bigr)=2\alpha\lVert A^T a\rVert_2.\] Consequently, \[w(E)\leq w(K)\leq\alpha w(E).\] Thus an \(\alpha\)-rounding preserves lattice width up to the multiplicative factor \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex body lies between concentric ellipsoids whose scale differs by alpha, its lattice width lies between the widths of those ellipsoids and therefore differs from the inner-ellipsoid width by at most the factor alpha.
assumptions_latex: \(E=c+A B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq c+\alpha A B_2^n\).
\(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(\alpha\geq 1\).
Lattice width is measured over \(a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(E)\leq w(K)\leq\alpha w(E)\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball in dimension n
width of C in direction a

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex body.
\(K\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(K)\leq f(n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the qualitative flatness theorem; no particular numerical bound for the flatness constant is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every dimension \(n\geq1\), there exists a finite constant \(f(n)\) such that every convex body \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(K\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\varnothing\) has lattice width \[w(K):=\min_{a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}}\left(\sup_{x\in K}a^Tx-\inf_{x\in K}a^Tx\right)\leq f(n).\] Equivalently, if \(w(K)>f(n)\), then \(K\) contains an integer point. The flat-body regime is therefore the case in which a short integral direction of bounded width is available for branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice-point-free convex body has width at most a dimension-dependent constant in some integral direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Body Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative flatness theorem is correctly scoped and theorem is an appropriate role for the regime-defining claim, but the nontrivial theorem has no source or locator.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
A primitive \(a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfies \(w_a(K)\leq W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integer feasibility in \(K\) reduces to at most \(\lfloor W\rfloor+1\) integer-feasibility problems of dimension \(n-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the dimension-reducing branch over integral hyperplanes orthogonal to a primitive flat direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Compute \(\ell=
\lceil\inf_{x\in K}a^Tx\rceil\) and \(u=\lfloor\sup_{x\in K}a^Tx\rfloor\). For each integer \(k\in\{\ell,
\ldots,u\}\), recursively test the slice \(K_k=K\cap\{x
\in\mathbb{R}^n:a^Tx=k\}\). Because \(a\) is primitive, an integer unimodular change of coordinates identifies the lattice in each nonempty slice with \(\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\). Stop when a recursive call returns a lattice point; report infeasibility if all calls fail. Since \(u-
\ell+1\leq\lfloor W\rfloor+1\), a dimension-only width bound gives dimension-only branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch over the finitely many integer hyperplanes crossing a flat body, transform each slice, and recurse in one lower dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Dimension Reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The slicing recursion and branch bound are mathematically plausible, but computation of the extrema and representation of recursive slices require an explicit input or oracle model. children.title: Fixed-Dimension Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Integer-feasibility complexity when the variable dimension is fixed.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(n\) is fixed.
The binary encoding length of \((A,b)\) is \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whether \(\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is empty is decidable in time polynomial in \(L\) for fixed \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical binary-encoded linear integer feasibility with the number of variables fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists an algorithm which, given \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), decides whether \(P_{
\mathbb{Z}}=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is empty. For every fixed \(n\), its running time and bit complexity are bounded by a polynomial in the binary encoding length \(L\) of \((A,b)\); the degree and multiplicative constants may depend on \(n\). Thus fixed dimension converts integer linear feasibility from a generally NP-hard problem into a polynomial-time task under the standard Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer linear feasibility is polynomial-time solvable in the binary input length when the number of variables is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Dimension Feasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-dimension polynomial-time claim and complexity-bound kind fit the leaf, but this central theorem is unsupported by any citation or theorem locator.

children.title: Fixed-Dimension Optimization
children.top_down_role: Objective optimization over fixed-dimensional integer feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is a bounded rational polyhedron and \(n\) is fixed.
\(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) and all data are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal \(x^*\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\), or infeasibility, is computable in polynomial time for fixed \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear integer optimization in fixed dimension under binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\), \(b\), and \(c\), one can either report \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=
\varnothing\) or return \(x^*\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\) satisfying \[c^Tx^*=\min\{c^Tx:x\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\}.\] For fixed \(n\), rational polyhedral bounds yield polynomial-bit lower and upper bounds on the integer objective. Binary search over integer thresholds, using feasibility for \(Ax\leq b\) together with \(c^Tx\leq\gamma\), locates the optimal value in polynomially many feasibility calls; constructive feasibility then returns an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded integer linear optimization is polynomial-time solvable in fixed dimension by threshold feasibility and witness recovery.

children.title: Feasibility–Optimization Transfer
children.top_down_role: Reductions between fixed-dimensional feasibility and optimization interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility–Optimization Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-to-optimization transfer for an integer-valued linear objective with known finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) be represented so that adding a linear inequality preserves the feasibility model, and let \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\). Suppose every \(x\in F\) satisfies \(L\leq c^Tx\leq U\), where \(L,U\in\mathbb{Z}\). First query feasibility of \(F_U=F\cap\{x:c^Tx\leq U\}\); if it is empty, report that \(F\) is empty. Otherwise, binary-search the smallest \(\gamma\in[L,U]\cap\mathbb{Z}\) for which \(F_\gamma=F\cap\{x:c^Tx\leq\gamma\}\) is nonempty. A constructive feasibility call on the minimum feasible threshold returns an optimizer. The reduction uses \(O(\log(U-L+1)+1)\) feasibility calls and one witness-recovery call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First test whether the feasible set is empty; otherwise binary-search the smallest feasible integer objective threshold and recover a witness at that threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is represented so that adding one linear inequality preserves the feasibility model.
\(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), so \(c^Tx\) is integer-valued on \(F\).
Known bounds \(L,U\in\mathbb{Z}\) satisfy \(L\leq c^Tx\leq U\) for every \(x\in F\).
A polynomial-time feasibility-and-witness routine is available for the augmented model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization or detection of infeasibility uses \(O(\log(U-L+1)+1)\) feasibility calls plus one witness-recovery call.

notation.meaning: integer lower and upper objective bounds

assumptions_latex: \(p\) is fixed, while \(q\) and the number of inequalities may vary.
All matrices and vectors are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mixed-integer linear feasibility and optimization are polynomial-time solvable when only the integer dimension \(p\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear mixed programs with fixed integer-variable count and unrestricted continuous-variable count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the rational mixed-integer linear program \[\min\{c^Tx+d^Ty:Ax+By\leq b,
\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^p,
\ y\in\mathbb{R}^q\}.\] When \(p\) is fixed, there is a Turing-polynomial algorithm in the binary input length that decides feasibility and, for a finite optimum, returns an optimal mixed-integer solution. The polynomial may depend on \(p\), but not exponentially on the varying continuous dimension \(q\). The algorithm must also distinguish infeasibility from objective unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear mixed-integer programs are polynomial-time solvable when the number of integer variables is fixed, even if continuous dimension varies.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Integer-Dimension Mixed Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the topic, but polynomial solvability with fixed integer dimension and unrestricted continuous dimension is a delicate theorem whose precise encoding, optimization, and unboundedness guarantees require an authoritative citation.

children.title: Convex Integer Extensions
children.top_down_role: Fixed-dimensional extensions with convex feasible regions or objectives.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is bounded and convex, with fixed \(n\).
Separation and value oracles have polynomial bit complexity and certified rational accuracy.
Explicit rational inner and outer radius bounds and an accuracy gap are supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The geometric fixed-dimension recursion extends when its separation, rounding, and lattice subproblems are polynomially implementable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient oracle interface for extending fixed-dimensional geometric methods from polyhedra to convex integer sets.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.3 Unconstrained convex integer program p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex integer problem \(\min\{f(x):x\in K\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\}\) admits a Lenstra-type fixed-dimensional extension when the input model permits, in polynomial bit complexity, separation of points from \(K\), comparison or separation of convex sublevel sets \(K\n\cap\{x:f(x)\leq\gamma\}\), and computation of sufficiently accurate ellipsoidal roundings. Certified rational inner and outer bounds must make weak oracle answers distinguishable at the requested accuracy. Under these interface conditions, feasibility at each objective threshold is a convex integer feasibility problem to which geometric rounding, lattice detection, and flat-direction recursion apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex integer extensions require effective separation, bounded geometry, controlled precision, and polynomially computable roundings in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Integer Extensions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.3 Unconstrained convex integer program p. 32

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited page is specific, but the available evidence does not establish that it supports the broad separation, precision, rounding, and bit-complexity interface asserted here. Terms such as sufficiently accurate are not quantified, and statement_latex also contains a malformed \n command before \cap.

children.title: Quasiconvex Integer Extensions
children.top_down_role: Fixed-dimensional extensions involving quasiconvex constraints or objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Integer Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-form conditions under which fixed-dimensional quasiconvex integer minimization admits Lenstra-type treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a bounded rational box and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:B\to\mathbb{R}\). A quasiconvex integer extension is algorithmically admissible when every sublevel set \(\{x\in B:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) and \(\{x\in B:g_i(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is convex, feasibility is \(x\in B\cap\mathbb{Z}^d\) with \(g_i(x)\leq0\), and polynomial-time strong separation oracles are available for all queried rational levels. For fixed \(d\), a Lenstra-type scheme may then optimize \(f\) by level-set feasibility, provided the oracle outputs and required accuracy have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-dimensional quasiconvex integer optimization extends the Lenstra framework when bounded sublevel sets are convex and support polynomial-time, polynomial-bit strong separation.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is fixed and \(B\) is a bounded rational box.
All relevant sublevel sets are convex.
Strong separation and value comparisons have polynomial cost and encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quasiconvex minimization reduces to fixed-dimensional convex integer feasibility over queried sublevel sets.

children.title: Convex Oracle Requirements

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Oracle Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal effective-oracle conditions for bounded fixed-dimensional convex integer feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), a Lenstra-type oracle formulation requires rational bounds \(K\subseteq[-R,R]^d\), a polynomial-time strong separation oracle, and polynomially bounded output size. Given rational \(y\), the oracle must either certify \(y\in K\) or return rational \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^Ty>\beta\) and \(a^Tx\leq\beta\) for every \(x\in K\). Any weak-oracle replacement must additionally specify geometric radii and an accuracy parameter sufficient to distinguish exact integer feasibility from approximation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex extension needs bounded geometry and an effective separation oracle; membership answers alone do not supply the cuts used by Lenstra-type recursion.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is convex and bounded by explicitly encoded rational data.
Oracle running time and output length are polynomial in the query and input sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned inequality is a polynomially representable valid cut separating \(y\) from \(K\).

children.title: Nonconvexity Failure Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvexity Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the quasiconvex level-set mechanism when convexity is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a constraint or objective sublevel set \(S_\alpha=\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is nonconvex, a separating inequality valid for all of \(S_\alpha\) need not exist at a queried point outside it. Consequently, the central Lenstra-type operation—replacing a failed query by a valid convex cut and applying lattice-width recursion—has no general justification. Fixed dimension alone therefore gives no polynomial-time guarantee for arbitrarily represented nonconvex integer problems; additional structure, such as a polynomial-size union of convex sets, is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convex sublevel sets, valid separating cuts may not exist, so the Lenstra recursion and its polynomial guarantee do not extend automatically.
assumptions_latex: At least one relevant sublevel or feasible set is nonconvex.
No alternative finite convex decomposition or comparable structure is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard separation-and-lattice-width Lenstra framework is not generally applicable.

notation.meaning: objective or constraint sublevel set at level alpha

knowledge_statements.title: Kannan Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical fixed-dimension improvement of Lenstra’s linear integer programming algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times d}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), and binary input length \(L\), Kannan's refinement decides whether \(\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d:Ax\leq b\}\) is empty and finds a feasible point when one exists in time \(d^{O(d)}\operatorname{poly}(L)\). Thus the exponent of \(L\) is independent of \(d\), while all superpolynomial dependence is confined to the dimension parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kannan refined fixed-dimensional linear integer programming to dimension cost d to the O(d), multiplied by a polynomial in binary input length.

The integer dimension \(d\) is the parameter; arithmetic bit costs are counted.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Reduction Refinements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Use of reduced lattice bases to sharpen branching directions in fixed-dimensional integer feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bounded rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), initialize with the lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^d\) under an ellipsoidal normalization of \(P\). Compute a polynomial-time reduced basis of the transformed lattice, select a short dual-lattice vector \(c\), and bound the integer values of \(c^Tx\) attained on \(P\). Branch on each integer hyperplane \(c^Tx=k\) in that interval, recursively reduce the dimension, and output the first feasible integer point; output infeasible when every branch is exhausted. Basis reduction controls coefficient growth and supplies an effectively computable thin direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced lattice basis exposes a short dual direction, enabling bounded hyperplane branching and controlled arithmetic in Lenstra-type recursion.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded, rational, and explicitly represented.
A polynomial-time lattice-basis reduction routine is used.
The dimension \(d\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursion either returns a point in \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^d\) or certifies that this set is empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Growing-Dimension Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of polynomial-time solvability when integer dimension belongs to the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fixed-dimension hypothesis cannot be dropped from the Lenstra-family guarantee. When \(d\) is part of the input, feasibility of \(Ax\leq b\), \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^d\), is NP-hard even after bounds \(0\leq x_i\leq1\) force every variable to be binary. Hence a bound of the form \(f(d)\operatorname{poly}(L)\) yields polynomial time only for fixed \(d\); it does not imply polynomial time in the combined input \((d,L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer linear feasibility becomes NP-hard when dimension grows, even for binary variables; Lenstra-family polynomiality is therefore strictly fixed-dimensional.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Representation Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Membership-Oracle Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information missing from bare membership access in cutting-plane implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A membership oracle for \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) returns only whether a query \(y\) belongs to \(K\). From a negative answer it supplies neither a normal \(a\) nor an offset \(\beta\) defining an inequality valid on all of \(K\). Therefore bare membership access does not directly implement the separating-cut step required by standard Lenstra-type convex algorithms. Any conversion must assume additional geometric data and an approximation model, and its query and precision costs must be included in the final complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership answers do not contain separating hyperplanes; using them in a Lenstra-type method requires extra geometry, approximation assumptions, and accounted simulation cost.

No separating hyperplane or geometric conditioning data are supplied.

children.title: Oracle Simulation Costs
children.top_down_role: Complexity overhead incurred when one access model simulates another.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Simulation Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for Lenstra iterations and simulated oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a fixed-dimensional Lenstra-type algorithm makes at most \(Q(d,L)\) calls to a strong separation oracle and performs \(H(d,L)\) additional bit operations. If each separation call can be simulated using at most \(q(d,L)\) primitive-oracle queries and \(T(d,L)\) bit operations, with polynomially bounded intermediate precision, then the total cost is at most \(Q(d,L)q(d,L)\) primitive queries and \(H(d,L)+Q(d,L)T(d,L)\) bit operations. Thus polynomiality is preserved only when the simulation cost and required precision are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle substitution multiplies query counts and adds per-call simulation work; hidden superpolynomial precision or simulation costs destroy the claimed polynomial bound.
assumptions_latex: The outer algorithm uses at most \(Q(d,L)\) separation calls.
Each simulated call uses at most \(q(d,L)\) primitive queries and \(T(d,L)\) bit operations.
Intermediate numbers have polynomially bounded encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composed costs are \(Qq\) primitive queries and \(H+QT\) bit operations.

notation.meaning: per-call simulation query and bit-operation bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Feasible-Region Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box obstruction showing that fixed dimension alone does not tame arbitrary nonconvex regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=2^L\) and consider the one-dimensional integer domain \(D_L=\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\). An unknown feasible set is promised to be either empty or a singleton \(\{s\}\subseteq D_L\), and access is only through membership queries. The set is generally nonconvex as a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\). Any deterministic algorithm deciding nonemptiness must, in the worst case, query all \(N\) points: after fewer queries, an unqueried point can be chosen as \(s\) without changing previous answers. Thus fixed dimension does not yield polynomial complexity for arbitrary nonconvex oracle representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even in dimension one, an arbitrary hidden singleton may require exponentially many membership queries, so fixed dimension cannot overcome unrestricted nonconvex representation.
assumptions_latex: Only membership-oracle access to the feasible set is available.
The coordinate bound \(N-1\) is encoded using \(L\) bits.
The algorithm is deterministic and must decide exact nonemptiness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case membership-query complexity is \(2^L\), although the ambient dimension equals \(1\).

notation.meaning: number of candidate integer points, equal to \(2^L\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\), enumerate every sign vector \(s\in\{-1,1\}^n\). For each \(s\), form the pointed rational cone \[K_s=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=0,\ s_i x_i\ge 0\text{ for all }i\}.\] Compute the unique minimal Hilbert basis \(H_s\) of the affine semigroup \(K_s\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Delete zero and duplicate vectors, and output \[G=\bigcup_{s\in\{-1,1\}^n}H_s.\] Then \(G\) is precisely the set of nonzero \(\sqsubseteq\)-minimal vectors in \(\ker_{\mathbb Z}(A)\), hence \(G=\mathcal G(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate integer-kernel Hilbert bases in all orthants and unite them. The resulting finite set is exactly the Graver basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every circuit vector is conformally indecomposable in the integer kernel, and therefore \[\mathcal C(A)\subseteq\mathcal G(A).\] Moreover, for every nonzero \(z\in\ker_{\mathbb R}(A)\), there exist circuits \(c^1,\ldots,c^k\in\mathcal C(A)\) and scalars \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k>0\) such that \[z=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j c^j,\qquad \lambda_jc^j\sqsubseteq z\text{ for every }j.\] The circuits may be chosen with \(k\le n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\). The inclusion can be strict because conformal minimality does not require support minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every circuit is a Graver element, while every real kernel direction is a positive conformal combination of circuits; the inclusion may be strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Circuit–Graver Relationship

children.title: Support-Minimality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where support minimality does not capture all required conformal directions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Support minimality is sufficient but not necessary for conformal minimality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed one-row matrix directly separates support minimality from conformal minimality
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary between circuit support minimality and Graver conformal minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=(1,-1,1)\). Then \(Ag=0\), but \(g\notin\mathcal C(A)\), because \(h=(1,0,-1)\) is a nonzero kernel vector with \(\operatorname{supp}(h)\subsetneq\operatorname{supp}(g)\). Nevertheless, \(g\in\mathcal G(A)\): if \(0\ne z\in\ker_{\mathbb Z}(A)\) and \(z\sqsubseteq g\), then \(z_1,z_3\in\{0,1\}\), \(z_2\in\{0,-1\}\), and \(z_1+2z_2+z_3=0\) forces \(z=g\). Hence Graver minimality cannot be replaced by support minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For A=(1,2,1), (1,-1,1) is Graver-minimal but not support-minimal, so Graver elements need not be circuits.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Minimality Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed matrix correctly separates support minimality from conformal minimality, and failure_boundary is the appropriate role for this leaf. Despite the directly checkable example, no inspectable citation is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\), and a monomial order in which larger \(c^T\)-value has precedence is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oriented exponent differences of the reduced Gröbner basis form an improving test set for every fiber of \(A\).

notation.meaning: reduced Gröbner basis under the fixed order

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oriented binomial exponent differences are the standard Gröbner test-set construction for integer-program fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative integer fibers and a cost-compatible monomial order are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every binomial \(X^u-X^v\in\mathcal B\) whose leading monomial is \(X^u\), orient the move as \(g=v-u\), and set \(T=\{v-u:X^u-X^v\in\mathcal B\}\). For any \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) and \(x\in\{z\in\mathbb N^n:Az=b\}\), either \(x\) is the order-minimal normal form in its fiber, or some \(g\in T\) satisfies \(x+g\in\mathbb N^n\), \(A(x+g)=b\), and \(c^T(x+g)<c^Tx\). Thus repeated Gröbner reduction reaches an optimal fiber representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-oriented differences from a reduced toric Gröbner basis provide feasible improving moves until the fiber's optimal normal form is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Gröbner Test Sets

children.title: Augmentation Method Family
children.top_down_role: Objective and oracle variants of test-set augmentation.

assumptions_latex: \(A,b,c,l,u\) are integral and \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty and finite.
A finite test set \(T\subseteq\ker_{\mathbb Z}(A)\setminus\{0\}\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is optimal whenever \(T\) is an improving test set for all nonoptimal points of \(F\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-test-set augmentation is the standard optimality procedure for bounded linear integer programs
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic augmentation with any finite improving test set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible point \(x^0\in F\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(g^k\in T\) and an integer \(\alpha_k\ge1\) such that \(x^k+\alpha_k g^k\in F\) and \(\alpha_k c^Tg^k<0\); optionally choose the pair giving the largest objective decrease. Set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_k g^k\). Stop when no such pair exists and output \(x^k\). Since the integral objective decreases strictly on the finite set \(F\), the procedure terminates. If every nonoptimal \(x\in F\) admits such a move from \(T\), the output minimizes \(c^Tx\) over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly take a feasible, objective-improving integer kernel move from a test set; absence of such a move certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Objective Augmentation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic finite-test-set augmentation algorithm is correct under its explicitly conditional improving-test-set hypothesis, and algorithm fits the leaf. No inspectable citation is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty and finite.
\(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\) is discrete convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(x^0\in F\) and \(\mathcal G(A)\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(g^k\in\mathcal G(A)\) and \(\alpha_k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) with \(x^k+\alpha_k g^k\in F\) and \(f(x^k+\alpha_k g^k)<f(x^k)\); a Graver-best rule minimizes \(f(x^k+\alpha g)\) over all feasible pairs. Set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_k g^k\). Stop when no improving pair exists. The conformal decomposition property and separable convexity imply that the terminal point is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use feasible improving Graver moves for a separable discrete-convex objective; no improving Graver move is an exact global optimality certificate.

children.title: Steepest-Descent Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Augmentation organized by steepness-based direction selection.

assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is finite and \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\).
A finite test set \(T\subseteq\ker_{\mathbb Z}(A)\setminus\{0\}\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration selects a feasible direction of greatest objective improvement per unit \(\ell_1\)-length and then takes a maximal step.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the normalized objective slope with a maximal feasible step is the standard discrete steepest-descent rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear minimization with \(\ell_1\)-normalized direction steepness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from \(x^0\in F\). At iteration \(k\), among all \(g\in T\) for which \(c^Tg<0\) and \(x^k+g\in F\), choose \(g^k\) maximizing \[\rho(g)=\frac{-c^Tg}{\lVert g\rVert_1}.\] Choose the maximal integer \(\alpha_k\ge1\) satisfying \(x^k+\alpha_k g^k\in F\), and set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_k g^k\). Stop when no improving feasible direction exists. If \(T\) is an exact test set, such as \(\mathcal G(A)\), return the resulting optimal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the feasible test-set direction with best objective decrease per unit one-norm, take its maximal feasible step, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.title: Steepest-Descent Augmentation

children.title: Scaling-Based Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Augmentation organized through successive objective or step-size scales.

assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is finite and \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\).
A test set \(T\subseteq\ker_{\mathbb Z}(A)\setminus\{0\}\) and feasible \(x^0\in F\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successive dyadic scales restrict accepted improvements, and the final unit-scale termination condition is exact for an exact test set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dyadic threshold reduction is the standard scaling template for integral augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic objective-improvement scaling scheme for integral linear objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\Delta=2^{\lceil\log_2 M\rceil}\), where \(M\ge1\) bounds the absolute objective difference between points of \(F\). At scale \(\Delta\), repeatedly choose \(g\in T\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that \(x+\alpha g\in F\) and \(-\alpha c^Tg\ge\Delta\), update \(x\leftarrow x+\alpha g\), and stop the phase when no such pair exists. Then set \(\Delta\leftarrow\Delta/2\). Terminate after completing scale \(\Delta=1\). Because objective differences are integral, if \(T\) detects every improving point, the output is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept augmentations exceeding a dyadic objective threshold, halve the threshold after each exhausted phase, and finish at unit improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Based Augmentation

children.title: Direction-Selection Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural tradeoffs between steepest and scaling choices.

assumptions_latex: \(x\) lies in a finite integer fiber \(F\), \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\), and \(T\) is a finite test set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Steepest, deepest, and scaled rules optimize different functions of the same feasible augmentation pairs and need not select the same direction.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the comparison follows directly from the displayed direction-selection objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison is local to one iterate and one common test set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Among pairs \((g,\alpha)\in P(x)\) with \(G(g,\alpha)>0\), a deepest-descent or Graver-best rule maximizes \(G(g,\alpha)\); a steepest-descent rule maximizes \(-c^Tg/\lVert g\rVert_1\) and conventionally takes the maximal feasible \(\alpha\) afterward; a scaling rule merely requires \(G(g,\alpha)\ge\Delta\) at the current threshold. Consequently, deepest selection controls one-step objective reduction, steepest selection controls reduction per unit direction length, and scaling controls admissibility by magnitude. These criteria are generally inequivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deepest descent maximizes total gain, steepest descent maximizes normalized directional gain, and scaling accepts any gain above its current threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Direction-Selection Comparison

children.title: Phase-Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Iteration and phase behavior under relevant parameter restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is finite and nonempty.
Arithmetic and comparisons are counted in the binary encoding model.
\(M=\max_{x,y\in F}|c^T(x-y)|\ge1\) for the stated dyadic phase count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dyadic scaling has logarithmically many magnitude phases, whereas maximal Graver steepest descent has a combinatorial augmentation bound independent of objective magnitudes.

notation.meaning: maximum absolute objective difference on F

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dyadic phase counting and the nonrepetition bound for maximal Graver steepest descent are standard augmentation analyses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts scaling phases and augmentation iterations, excluding oracle implementation cost; the displayed scaling count assumes nonzero objective range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a dyadic scaling algorithm starts at \(2^{\lceil\log_2 M\rceil}\) and halves through scale \(1\), it executes at most \(1+\lceil\log_2 M\rceil\) phases. Thus its phase count is polynomial in the binary length of \(M\), although an iteration bound per phase remains necessary. For linear minimization using \(T=\mathcal G(A)\), steepest-direction selection with maximal feasible steps never reuses a Graver direction; hence it performs at most \(|\mathcal G(A)|\) augmentations. This latter bound is independent of \(\lVert c\rVert_\infty\) but may be large when the matrix family does not bound \(|\mathcal G(A)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling uses logarithmically many objective-magnitude phases; maximal Graver steepest descent uses at most one augmentation per Graver direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Phase-Complexity Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^m:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\neq\varnothing\).
\(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is the objective to be minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O(x)=\bot\) certifies optimality, while \(\mathcal O(x)=g\) supplies a feasible strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact improvement oracle for a bounded integer feasible set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An augmentation oracle for minimizing \(f\) over \(F\) is a map \(\mathcal O:F\to\mathbb Z^m\cup\{\bot\}\) such that, for every \(x\in F\), either \(\mathcal O(x)=g\) with \(g\neq0\), \(x+g\in F\), and \(f(x+g)<f(x)\), or \(\mathcal O(x)=\bot\). An exact oracle may return \(\bot\) only when \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in F\). Thus repeated oracle calls produce strict feasible improvements and terminate at an optimum whenever \(F\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact augmentation oracle either returns a feasible improving integer direction or certifies that the current feasible point is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation Oracles

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graver-Basis Criterion for Finiteness of Integer Fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general Graver-basis recession criterion for fibers with possibly infinite coordinate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), let \(\mathcal G(A)\) be its Graver basis, and let \(l,u\in\mathbb Z_\infty^n\). If there exists \(g\in\mathcal G(A)\) such that \(g_i\le 0\) whenever \(u_i<\infty\) and \(g_i\ge 0\) whenever \(l_i> -\infty\), then, for every \(b\), \(S_b:=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is either empty or infinite. If no such \(g\) exists, every such \(S_b\) is finite. Given \(\mathcal G(A),l,u\), the existence of such a vector is decidable in time polynomial in \(\langle\mathcal G(A),l,u\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Graver vector with the stated signs characterizes whether nonempty integer fibers under the given possibly infinite bounds are infinite; the condition is polynomially checkable when the Graver basis is explicit.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}
\mathcal G(A)\text{ is the explicitly given Graver basis of }A
l,u\in\mathbb Z_\infty^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\exists g\in\mathcal G(A)\text{ satisfying the stated sign conditions}\right)\Rightarrow\forall b,\ S_b\text{ is empty or infinite};\quad\left(\nexists g\right)\Rightarrow\forall b,\ S_b\text{ is finite}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The standard n-fold matrix generated by \(D\) and \(A\) is
\[E^{(n)}=\begin{pmatrix}D&D&\cdots&D\\ A&0&\cdots&0\\0&A&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb Z^{(r+ns)\times nt}.\]
A standard n-fold integer program minimizes a linear or separable convex objective \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x^i)\) subject to \(E^{(n)}x=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), and \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\in\mathbb Z^{nt}\). The first block row imposes global coupling constraints, and each remaining block row imposes local constraints on one brick.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard n-fold program repeats fixed local constraints on each brick and couples all bricks through one repeated global block row.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Separable Convex n-Fold Integer Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-model complexity guarantee for separable convex minimization over a fixed standard n-fold structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every fixed integer $(r,s)\times t$ bimatrix $A$, there is an algorithm which, given $n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, $l,u\in\mathbb Z_\infty^{nt}$, $b\in\mathbb Z^{r+ns}$, and a separable convex function $f:\mathbb Z^{nt}\to\mathbb Z$ presented by a comparison oracle, solves
\[
\min\{f(x):x\in\mathbb Z^{nt},\ A^{(n)}x=b,\ l\le x\le u\}
\]
in time polynomial in $n$ and $\langle l,u,b,\widehat f\rangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed integer bimatrix A, a separable convex objective supplied through a comparison oracle can be minimized over a bounded standard n-fold integer system in time polynomial in n and the stated encoding parameters.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is a fixed integer }(r,s)\times t\text{ bimatrix}
n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}
l,u\in\mathbb Z_\infty^{nt}
b\in\mathbb Z^{r+ns}
f:\mathbb Z^{nt}\to\mathbb Z\text{ is separable convex and presented by a comparison oracle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{f(x):x\in\mathbb Z^{nt},\ A^{(n)}x=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\text{ is solvable in time }\operatorname{poly}(n,\langle l,u,b,\widehat f\rangle).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the block matrix underlying standard n-fold integer-programming models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An $(r,s)\times t$ bimatrix is a matrix $A$ partitioned into an $r\times t$ block $A_1$ formed by its first $r$ rows and an $s\times t$ block $A_2$ formed by its last $s$ rows. For $n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, its $n$-fold product is
\[
A^{(n)}:=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&A_1&\cdots&A_1\\A_2&0&\cdots&0\\0&A_2&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A_2\end{pmatrix},
\]
a matrix of size $(r+ns)\times nt$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An (r,s)-by-t bimatrix consists of an r-by-t block A1 above an s-by-t block A2. Its n-fold product has n copies of A1 across the top block row and n copies of A2 along the lower block diagonal, giving dimensions (r+ns)-by-nt.
assumptions_latex: r,s,t,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}
A_1\text{ has size }r\times t
A_2\text{ has size }s\times t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{(n)}\text{ has size }(r+ns)\times nt\text{, with repeated top block }A_1\text{ and block-diagonal blocks }A_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A huge n-fold model is a compressed n-fold instance in which bricks are specified by types rather than individually. Type \(k\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\) occurs \(n_k\) times and prescribes its local block, bounds, right-hand side, and objective contribution. Its expanded variables are \(x^{k,j}\in\mathbb Z^t\) for \(1\le j\le n_k\); they satisfy \(A_kx^{k,j}=b_k\), \(\ell_k\le x^{k,j}\le u_k\), and the coupling equation \(\sum_{k=1}^q\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}D_kx^{k,j}=b^0\). The objective is \(\sum_{k=1}^q\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}f_k(x^{k,j})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A huge n-fold model represents exponentially many repeated bricks by listing finitely many brick types and binary-encoded multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.title: Huge n-Fold Models

assumptions_latex: \(C\in\mathbb Z^{p\times q}\), \(D\in\mathbb Z^{p\times t}\), \(B\in\mathbb Z^{s\times q}\), and \(A\in\mathbb Z^{s\times t}\).
\(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The four-block n-fold matrix determined by \(C,D,B,A\) is
\[H^{(n)}=\begin{pmatrix}C&D&D&\cdots&D\\B&A&0&\cdots&0\\B&0&A&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\B&0&0&\cdots&A\end{pmatrix}.\]
Its columns are partitioned as \(x=(x^0,x^1,\ldots,x^n)\), where \(x^0\) is global and the \(x^i\) are local bricks. A four-block n-fold integer program imposes \(H^{(n)}x=b\), componentwise bounds, and integrality. The top block row couples all variables, while local row \(i\) couples \(x^0\) only with \(x^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A four-block n-fold model adds global variables that participate in both the global coupling rows and every repeated local row block.

children.title: n-Fold Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Augmentation methods specialized to standard n-fold block structure.

assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^{nt}:E^{(n)}x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\neq\varnothing\) is finite.
An exact augmentation oracle is available for the objective \(f\) on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-based augmentation scheme for a finite n-fold feasible set.

source_refs.locator: Theory and applications of n-fold integer programming p. 559

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an n-fold instance and a feasible point \(x^0\in F\). For iterations \(k=0,1,\ldots\), query the exact augmentation oracle at \(x^k\). If it returns \(\bot\), stop and output \(x^k\). Otherwise it returns \(g^k\neq0\) satisfying \(x^k+g^k\in F\) and \(f(x^k+g^k)<f(x^k)\); set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+g^k\). Because \(F\) is finite and every accepted step strictly decreases the objective, the method terminates. Exactness of the oracle makes the terminal point globally optimal over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible n-fold solution, repeatedly apply exact feasible improvements; stop when the oracle certifies that no improving augmentation exists.
knowledge_statements.title: n-Fold Augmentation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Superadditivity of Same-Sign Convex Increments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A univariate convexity inequality whose canonical home is convex analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be convex, let \(r\in\mathbb R\), and let \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(s_i s_j\ge 0\) for all \(i,j\). Then \[f\!\left(r+\sum_{i=1}^m s_i\right)-f(r)\ge\sum_{i=1}^m\left(f(r+s_i)-f(r)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For displacements all having the same sign, the convex-function increment from their sum is at least the sum of their separate increments from the same base point.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex}
r,s_1,\ldots,s_m\in\mathbb R
s_i s_j\ge 0\quad\forall i,j
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\!\left(r+\sum_{i=1}^m s_i\right)-f(r)\ge\sum_{i=1}^m\left(f(r+s_i)-f(r)\right).

children.title: n-Fold Proximity Bounds
children.top_down_role: Distance controls linking continuous or relaxed solutions to integer solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^{nt}:E^{(n)}x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty and bounded.
The integer feasible set \(F=P\cap\mathbb Z^{nt}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(z^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in F}c^\top z\) with \(\lVert z^*-x^*\rVert\le\rho\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic proximity property; the sharp n-fold radius is source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An n-fold proximity bound is a number \(\rho\), stated as an explicit function of the block dimensions, coefficient bound, number of bricks, and chosen norm, with the following property. For every integral right-hand side, integral bounds, and cost vector \(c\), and for a specified optimal vertex \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^\top x\), there is an integer optimum \(z^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in F}c^\top z\) satisfying \(\lVert z^*-x^*\rVert\le\rho\). The norm and dependence of \(\rho\) must be fixed when invoking the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximity bound guarantees an optimal integer n-fold solution within a stated norm-radius of a specified optimal vertex of the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: n-Fold Proximity Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines a generic proximity property but supplies no n-fold-specific radius, norm, parameter dependence, or authoritative citation. A leaf titled n-Fold Proximity Bounds requires a sourced theorem, property, or explicit bound rather than a placeholder definition.

children.title: Augmentation–Proximity Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of proximity information to localize augmentation searches.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb Z^{nt}\) is a nonempty finite feasible set and \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is minimized over \(F\).
A relaxation optimum \(x^*\in\mathbb R^{nt}\), a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\), and \(\rho\ge0\) satisfy: some \(z^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in F}f(z)\) obeys \(\lVert z^*-x^*\rVert\le\rho\).
An exact augmentation oracle for \(f\) is available on the restricted feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact augmentation over \(F_\rho\) terminates at a point minimizing \(f\) over the original set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction by a stated proximity guarantee followed by exact augmentation on a finite feasible set.

source_refs.locator: Theory and applications of n-fold integer programming p. 559
2.4 Proximity between Continuous Solution and Integer Solution p. 28

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_\rho=\{z\in F:\lVert z-x^*\rVert\le\rho\}\). The proximity hypothesis gives an original optimum \(z^*\in F_\rho\), and therefore \(\min_{z\in F_\rho}f(z)=\min_{z\in F}f(z)\). Starting from any point of \(F_\rho\), repeatedly apply an exact augmentation oracle restricted to \(F_\rho\). Because \(F_\rho\) is finite, strict improvements terminate; when the oracle returns \(\bot\), its exactness certifies a minimizer over \(F_\rho\), which is also a minimizer over \(F\). Complexity bounds additionally require the costs of computing \(x^*\), finding an initial point in \(F_\rho\), and performing the augmentation calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximity guarantee places an original integer optimum in a finite restricted neighborhood, so exact augmentation within that neighborhood terminates at an optimum of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation–Proximity Interface

children.title: Parameter-Dependence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dependence on block dimensions, coefficient size, and structural parameters.

assumptions_latex: \(r,s,t\) are block dimensions, \(\Delta=\max\{|E_{ij}|\}\), and \(n\) is the brick count.
\(L\) denotes the binary encoding length of all numerical data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Claims of polynomiality or fixed-parameter tractability must identify which of \((r,s,t,\Delta,n,L)\) belong to the parameter and which belong to the input size.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity terminology for varying n-fold structural parameters.

source_refs.locator: Theory and applications of n-fold integer programming p. 559
Chapter 10. Sizes and the theoretical complexity of linear inequalities and linear programming p. 120
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For n-fold integer programming, the fixed-template regime treats \(r,s,t,\Delta\) as constants and measures running time in \(n\) and \(L\). A parameterized regime permits these structural quantities to vary and calls a bound fixed-parameter tractable only if it has the form \(f(r,s,t,\Delta)\operatorname{poly}(n,L)\) for a computable function \(f\). In the unrestricted regime, the block dimensions and coefficients contribute normally to \(L\), so a bound polynomial only for fixed blocks does not establish polynomial-time solvability. Unary versus binary encoding must also be stated for multiplicities and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An n-fold runtime claim must distinguish fixed block templates, parameterized blocks, and unrestricted input, while stating binary encoding and all parameter dependence.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Dependence Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a finite scenario set.
\(x\in\mathbb Z^{q}\) is chosen before the scenario and \(y_s\in\mathbb Z^{t_s}\) after observing \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic equivalent has a shared first-stage column block and scenario-diagonal recourse blocks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario deterministic equivalent with integer recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A two-stage stochastic integer program with finite scenarios has deterministic equivalent
\[\min\ c^\top x+\sum_{s\in S}p_s q_s^\top y_s\quad\text{subject to}\quad T_sx+W_sy_s=h_s\ \ (s\in S),\]
with prescribed componentwise bounds and integrality on \(x\) and each \(y_s\), where \(p_s\ge0\) and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\). The same first-stage vector \(x\) appears in every scenario constraint, whereas \(y_s\) appears only in scenario \(s\). This shared-versus-diagonal pattern is the two-stage stochastic block structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The deterministic equivalent shares one first-stage integer decision across scenarios and assigns each scenario its own diagonal recourse variables and constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Stochastic Integer Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic-equivalent representation is mathematically standard and internally consistent, but the record has no inspectable citation. Standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy the statement review's citation requirement.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is a finite rooted scenario tree of depth \(K\).
Each node \(v\) carries an integer decision \(x_v\) made from information available at \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Variables shared by scenarios with a common history enforce nonanticipativity automatically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-variable scenario-tree representation with integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite multistage stochastic integer program assigns one variable vector \(x_v\in\mathbb Z^{t_v}\) to each node \(v\) of a rooted scenario tree \(\mathcal T\). For every leaf \(\lambda\), its scenario constraints have the form \(\sum_{v\in P(\lambda)}A_{\lambda v}x_v=b_\lambda\), together with nodewise bounds, where \(P(\lambda)\) is the root-to-leaf path. The objective is the probability-weighted sum of node or leaf costs. Scenarios sharing a node use the same \(x_v\); hence decisions coincide until their histories branch, which is precisely the nonanticipativity requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multistage model places integer decisions on scenario-tree nodes; scenarios share decisions along their common history and diverge only after branching.
knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Stochastic Integer Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The node-variable explanation of nonanticipativity is plausible, but the leaf-wise constraint convention and probability-weighted objective require a specialized multistage stochastic integer-programming source.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is a finite rooted tree whose leaves index variable bricks.
Each depth \(d\) has a compatible integer row template \(A_d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every row block couples exactly the leaf bricks descending from its tree node.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hierarchical descendant-block description of tree-fold structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-fold integer-programming matrix is organized by a rooted tree \(\mathcal T\). Its column blocks are indexed by leaves \(\lambda\), with integer variables \(x_\lambda\). For each node \(v\) at depth \(d\), the associated row block has copies of a template \(A_d\) in precisely the columns indexed by descendant leaves \(L(v)\), and zeros elsewhere. Thus its equation is \(\sum_{\lambda\in L(v)}A_dx_\lambda=b_v\). Constraints at the root couple all bricks, while deeper constraints couple successively smaller subtrees; leaf constraints are local.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree-fold program nests repeated coupling constraints along a rooted tree, with each node constraining exactly the variable bricks in its descendant leaves.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Fold Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The descendant-leaf description plausibly captures a tree-fold hierarchy, but exact tree-fold matrix conventions vary. No source is supplied to verify the depth templates, row placement, or leaf-block convention.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is the constraint matrix of an integer program.
The primal graph joins columns that occur together with nonzero coefficients in some row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program has bounded primal treedepth when \(\operatorname{td}(G_P(A))\le d\) for a prescribed bound \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural definition via the column-intersection graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A program has bounded primal treedepth when the graph connecting variables that share a constraint admits a bounded-height rooted-forest closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Primal-Treedepth Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal graph and graph-treedepth definitions are precise, consistent, and appropriately classified as a definition, but the record lacks the required inspectable source for its application to integer programs.

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) has finite entries.
The integer program has the form \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program has dual treedepth at most \(d\) exactly when \(\operatorname{td}(G_D(A))\le d\).

notation.meaning: Dual interaction graph whose vertices are rows of \(A\), with two distinct rows adjacent when they share a nonzero column.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the row-intersection graph convention for dual treedepth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), define the dual graph \(G_D(A)\) on vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) by joining distinct rows \(i\) and \(j\) whenever some column \(k\) satisfies \(A_{ik}\ne0\) and \(A_{jk}\ne0\). The dual treedepth of \(A\) is \(\operatorname{td}_D(A):=\operatorname{td}(G_D(A))\). A family of integer programs \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) has bounded dual treedepth if there exists a constant \(d\) such that \(\operatorname{td}_D(A)\le d\) for every instance in the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual treedepth is the treedepth of the constraint-row intersection graph; a program family is bounded when this quantity has a uniform constant bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Dual-Treedepth Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the bounded dual-treedepth container and consistently uses the row-intersection convention, but no inspectable source is supplied to confirm that convention. Authoritative support with a specific definition, theorem, section, or page locator is required.

assumptions_latex: The constraint matrix is \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program is treewidth-bounded under a stated convention when the corresponding interaction graph has uniformly bounded treewidth.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes primal and dual matrix-interaction treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), let \(G_P(A)\) have the columns as vertices, adjacent when they occur nonzero in a common row, and let \(G_D(A)\) have the rows as vertices, adjacent when they occur nonzero in a common column. Define \(\operatorname{tw}_P(A):=\operatorname{tw}(G_P(A))\) and \(\operatorname{tw}_D(A):=\operatorname{tw}(G_D(A))\). A family of integer programs is primal-treewidth-bounded, respectively dual-treewidth-bounded, if one constant bounds \(\operatorname{tw}_P(A)\), respectively \(\operatorname{tw}_D(A)\), across all its instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treewidth-based integer programs bound the treewidth of a specified column- or row-interaction graph of every constraint matrix in the family.
knowledge_statements.title: Treewidth-Based Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition appropriately distinguishes primal and dual interaction-graph treewidth and fits the container. No inspectable source supports the terminology or conventions, so the record remains source-dependent.

assumptions_latex: Instances are encoded in binary and share a fixed structural decomposition.
A claimed algorithm has running time \(f(s,\Delta)\operatorname{poly}(L)\), where \(s\) measures structure and \(\Delta\) bounds local numerical data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\Delta\) is unbounded, this expression does not yield fixed-parameter tractability in \(s\) alone.

notation.meaning: Maximum absolute value of locally bounded coefficients, right-hand sides, or block data used by the algorithmic bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A parameterization failure, not an unconditional hardness claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an algorithmic guarantee \(T(I)\le f(s(I),\Delta(I))\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\), where \(s\) is a block-structure parameter and \(\Delta\) bounds numerical data used locally by the augmentation or dynamic-programming procedure. If a class satisfies \(s(I)\le s_0\) but permits \(\Delta(I)\) to grow without bound, then the displayed guarantee cannot be rewritten as \(g(s(I))\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\) merely from these assumptions. Thus bounded structure alone does not establish fixed-parameter tractability through this bound; a separate dependence analysis or encoding-sensitive argument is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an algorithm depends nonpolynomially on local coefficient bounds, allowing those bounds to grow destroys the claimed parameterization by structure alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Local Data

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the container, and the statement correctly limits itself to failure of an FPT inference rather than asserting hardness. A source is still needed for the underlying structured algorithm and its stated dependence on local numerical data.

assumptions_latex: A structured algorithm has running time \(f(d)\operatorname{poly}(L)\), where \(d\) is a decomposition depth.
No uniform upper bound on \(d\) is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bound \(f(d)\operatorname{poly}(L)\) alone does not imply polynomial time on the unrestricted-depth class.

notation.meaning: Depth of the relevant block, primal, or dual decomposition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records loss of a bounded-depth guarantee without asserting hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a family of structured integer programs admits an algorithm with running time \(T(I)\le f(d(I))\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\), where \(d(I)\) is the depth of the matrix decomposition and \(f\) is not known to be polynomially bounded in the encoded instance size. On a larger class allowing \(d(I)\to\infty\), this estimate supplies neither a uniform constant factor nor, by itself, a polynomial-time bound in \(L(I)\). Consequently the bounded-depth algorithmic conclusion cannot be transferred to the unrestricted-depth class without an additional bound on \(f(d(I))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depth-parameter algorithm does not automatically remain polynomial when decomposition depth grows with the input; this observation alone does not prove hardness.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Structure Depth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a valid failure-boundary observation and does not overstate hardness. However, no source identifies the applicable structured algorithm, depth parameter, or running-time dependence, so the intended local mathematical setting cannot be verified.

assumptions_latex: Each instance is partitioned into blocks \(B_1,\dots,B_t\).
The applicable structured bound depends on the maximum block dimension \(r:=\max_i\dim(B_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(r\) is unbounded, the bound does not establish tractability parameterized only by the number or incidence pattern of blocks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns loss of uniform block-size parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance be decomposed into blocks \(B_1,\dots,B_t\), and let \(r(I):=\max_i\dim(B_i)\). Suppose the available algorithmic estimate is \(T(I)\le f(r(I),s(I))\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\), with \(s\) describing the block-incidence pattern. If \(s(I)\le s_0\) while \(r(I)\) is allowed to grow, this estimate does not imply a bound of the form \(g(s(I))\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\). Hence nonuniform block growth lies outside the guarantee requiring uniformly bounded block dimensions, unless the dependence on \(r\) is separately controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Growing block dimensions invalidate guarantees that treat block size as fixed, even if the number or incidence pattern of blocks remains structured.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Block Growth

children.title: Counting Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Geometric and logical variants of exact lattice-point counting.

assumptions_latex: The polytope \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) is rational and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The count is \(N(P)=|P\cap\mathbb Z^d|=F_P(1,\dots,1)\), where the evaluation is finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generating-polynomial representation for a bounded rational polytope.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) be a bounded rational polytope. Its lattice-point generating function is the Laurent polynomial \[F_P(z):=\sum_{x\in P\cap\mathbb Z^d}z^x,\qquad z^x:=\prod_{i=1}^d z_i^{x_i}.\] Boundedness makes \(P\cap\mathbb Z^d\) finite, so substitution at \(z=(1,\dots,1)\) is ordinary polynomial evaluation and gives \[N(P):=|P\cap\mathbb Z^d|=F_P(1,\dots,1).\] Thus bounded-polytope counting is extraction of the total coefficient mass of \(F_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded rational polytope has finitely many lattice points, and their number is the value at all ones of its generating polynomial.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Polytope Counting

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Integer Programming p. 1

assumptions_latex: The rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) may be unbounded.
Generating functions are interpreted as formal Laurent series in a convergence cone or as rational functions after continuation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When a rational-function representation exists, it may encode \(P\cap\mathbb Z^d\) even though evaluation at \(z=\mathbf 1\) is generally undefined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal or rational-function semantics replace finite evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), define formally \[F_P(z):=\sum_{x\in P\cap\mathbb Z^d}z^x.\] If \(P\) is unbounded, this sum is generally infinite. A rational-function representation, when valid under the chosen convergence or formal-series convention, encodes the same coefficient indicator and typically has terms with denominators \(1-z^u\), where \(u\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^d\) is a recession direction. In contrast with bounded-polytope counting, direct substitution \(z=(1,\dots,1)\) is generally singular and does not represent a finite total count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded polyhedron may have an infinite lattice-point series represented rationally, but evaluation at all ones is generally singular and not a finite count.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Polyhedron Generating Functions

children.title: Projected-Set Counting
children.top_down_role: Counting distinct images produced by coordinate or linear projection.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^{p+q}\) is finite.
The map \(\pi(x,y)=x\) is the coordinate projection onto \(\mathbb Z^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projected-set counting returns \(|\pi(S)|\), counting each projected value once regardless of fiber size.

notation.meaning: Coordinate projection onto the first component.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite coordinate projections; multiplicities are discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^{p+q}\) be finite and let \(\pi:\mathbb Z^{p+q}\to\mathbb Z^p\) be given by \(\pi(x,y)=x\). The projected set is \[\pi(S)=\{x\in\mathbb Z^p:\exists y\in\mathbb Z^q\text{ with }(x,y)\in S\}.\] Projected-set counting asks for \(|\pi(S)|\). Equivalently, with fiber \(S_x:=\{y\in\mathbb Z^q:(x,y)\in S\}\), \[|\pi(S)|=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^p}\mathbf1_{\{|S_x|>0\}}.\] Thus different points in one nonempty fiber contribute only one projected value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected-set counting counts distinct projected integer vectors, so every nonempty fiber contributes one regardless of how many points it contains.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Set Counting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition precisely distinguishes distinct projected values from fiber multiplicity and fits the terminal container. No source with a specific locator is supplied, so the record cannot pass evidence review.

children.title: Parametric Fiber Counting
children.top_down_role: Counting lattice points in fibers indexed by external parameters.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^{p+q}\) has finite fibers under \(\pi(x,y)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parametric counting function is \(g(x)=|S_x|=\sum_y\mathbf 1_S(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts points within each finite parameter fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^{p+q}\) and regard \(x\in\mathbb Z^p\) as a parameter. For each \(x\), define the fiber \[S_x:=\{y\in\mathbb Z^q:(x,y)\in S\}.\] If every \(S_x\) is finite, the parametric fiber-counting function is \[g:\mathbb Z^p\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\qquad g(x):=|S_x|=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^q}\mathbf 1_S(x,y).\] Its support is precisely the projection of \(S\): \(\operatorname{supp}(g)=\{x:g(x)>0\}=\pi(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parametric fiber counting assigns to each parameter the number of feasible integer witnesses; its positive support is exactly the projected feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Fiber Counting

children.title: Projection–Parameter Interaction
children.top_down_role: Effects of projection on parameter chambers and fiber behavior.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^{p+q}\) has finite fibers.
The projection is \(\pi(x,y)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection indicator satisfies \(\mathbf 1_{\pi(S)}(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{g(x)>0\}}\), while \(g(x)\) retains fiber multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existential projection from multiplicity-sensitive fiber counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^{p+q}\) with finite fibers \(S_x:=\{y\in\mathbb Z^q:(x,y)\in S\}\), let \(g(x):=|S_x|\) and let \(\pi(x,y):=x\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb Z^p\), \[x\in\pi(S)\iff S_x\ne\varnothing\iff g(x)>0,\] and hence \[\mathbf 1_{\pi(S)}(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{g(x)>0\}}.\] Consequently \[|\pi(S)|=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^p}\mathbf 1_{\{g(x)>0\}}\] whenever \(\pi(S)\) is finite, whereas \[|S|=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^p}g(x)\] whenever \(S\) is finite. Projection therefore thresholds fiber counts instead of preserving their multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection records whether each fiber is nonempty, whereas parametric counting records its size; thresholding the fiber-count function produces the projection indicator.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Parameter Interaction

children.title: Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dimension, quantifier, and representation regimes governing tractability.

assumptions_latex: Input sets are represented by rational inequalities or short rational generating functions.
Complexity is measured in binary input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No polynomial-time claim follows without fixing dimension and specifying projection, quantifier, and output-representation parameters.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks parameter sensitivity without asserting an unsourced hardness classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For projection and parametric lattice-point counting, an algorithmic bound of the form \(f(d,q)\operatorname{poly}(L)\), where \(d\) is ambient dimension and \(q\) summarizes projected dimensions or quantifier structure, establishes polynomial time only on classes where \(d\) and \(q\) are fixed or otherwise controlled and the output representation is specified. If these parameters are part of the input and unbounded, the same estimate does not establish polynomial-time solvability in \(L\). Likewise, polynomial-delay enumeration, explicit output, and compact generating-function output are distinct complexity requirements and cannot be interchanged silently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting complexity depends on dimension, projection or quantifier structure, and output format; fixed-parameter results do not automatically extend when these features grow.
knowledge_statements.title: Complexity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and the statement carefully avoids claiming a hardness threshold. A precise source is nevertheless required to identify the relevant algorithmic bound, controlled parameters, encoding model, and output representations.

children.title: Semilinear-Set Counting
children.top_down_role: Counting from unions of linear-set representations.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) is represented as a finite union of linear sets.
The requested count is restricted to a finite region \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite counting quantity is \(|S\cap B|\), equivalently the sum of its membership indicator over \(B\).

notation.meaning: A linear set with base \(a\) and period vectors \(v_1,\dots,v_k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed counting for finitely represented semilinear subsets of \(\mathbb Z^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear set in \(\mathbb Z^d\) is \[L(a;v_1,\dots,v_k):=\left\{a+\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_jv_j:\lambda_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\right\},\] where \(a,v_1,\dots,v_k\in\mathbb Z^d\). A semilinear set is a finite union \[S=\bigcup_{i=1}^rL(a_i;v_{i1},\dots,v_{ik_i}).\] Because \(S\) may be infinite, finite semilinear-set counting requires a finite window \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) and returns \[N_S(B):=|S\cap B|=\sum_{x\in B}\mathbf 1_S(x).\] Overlaps among the displayed linear components are counted only once.
